It wasn’t pretty then and hasn’t been thus far. Nevertheless, more wins than losses is always a good thing. Strong defensive performances and penchant for fourth quarter heroics have continued […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - OCTOBER 15: Head coach Sean Payton of the Denver Broncos looks on against the Seattle Seahawks during the second quarter of the game at Empower Field At Mile High on October 15, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images After their first six games of the 2026 season, the Denver Broncos find themselves in familiar territory. They sport a 4-2 record—just like last season. It wasn’t pretty then and hasn’t been thus far. Nevertheless, more wins than losses is always a good thing. Strong defensive performances and penchant for fourth quarter heroics have continued for this year’s Broncos. This weekend, they face off against the Arizona Cardinals who are currently 2-4 and coming off an impressive victory the Los Angeles Rams. Even though the Cardinals have a losing record, the Broncos aren’t overlooking their Week 7 opponent. Each game provides an opportunity for every team in the National Football League. For the Broncos this Sunday, it’s a chance to get an important fifth win of the season. Moreover, it could become a streak starter. A gridiron battle—if won—that would give them confidence and momentum as the second half of the season approaches. Yesterday after practice, Head Coach Sean Payton touched based on a variety of topics. However, finding a way to improve and string together more victories to go on a run [like last year] was a point of emphasis. “That 4-2 mark a year ago, we’d come off of a real good defensive effort in London. It just can’t be a yo-yo. Any team that I can think of, there are runs. I think more importantly the last thing I just said to them was, ‘We have to be ascending, improving.’ I think they understand that,” stated Payton. The Broncos haven’t played a complete game thus far. Interestingly enough quite similar to 2025. The major exception being the matchup versus the Cincinnati Bengals who were without star quarterback Joe Burrow. There is no doubt Payton’s right. Denver needs to keep pushing forward and make the necessary adjustments to become a more complete team that’s built to compete for the long haul. A huge part of that is finding a viable recipe for success offensively. Broncos Country has grown accustomed to slowing starts on offense the past several years, only to find relief in the second half of the season when things finally started to click. Though with a little extra preparation for their Week 7 matchup, the team hopes that spark comes sooner than later. The Cardinals may not have a lot of star power on defense and rank in the bottom half of most metrics across the board. However, they put together a quality outing against the Los Angeles Rams last weekend. They give a lot of different looks and switch up a lot between Cover 3, Cover 4, and Cover 6 coverage looks—zone principles that Bo Nix and Denver’s offense are failing to find ways to beat. In order for the offense to do better, Payton acknowledged that it will be critical to be able to decipher and adequately react to their unique defensive packages. “Our defense, we see a base-look, kind of an Okie structure. There’ll be some similarities. Then they have a nickel package, a dime. Their penny—and we have a penny too—it can be a little blurry. One of the important notes this week was Communication ID,” mentioned Payton. “Usually there’s someone in the huddle that’s looking, and Bo is stepping into the huddle. They’re saying, ‘Nickel, nickel,’ or ‘Base, base.’ Then I’ll a lot of times say, ‘Hey Bo, this is base defense here.’ When we’re game planning, if you’re wanting to run a play against their base defense, there are certain things in order to know you’re getting base. There’s no 100 percent. That’s an important thing this week,” added Payton. How the Broncos choose to combat Arizona’s defense will be interesting to watch. Everyone is hoping to see Nix dial it up through the air, yet the biggest weakness the Cardinals have defensively is stopping the run. They’ve given up over 140 yards in three contests thus far. I think a big part of their game plan will be a healthy dose of J.K. Dobbins, RJ Harvey, and giving reps to Jonah Coleman who is expected to play on Sunday. If Denver can establish a formidable rushing attack, that would bode well for Nix and the offense, who have thrived off play-action principles and deep shots when the running game is clicking. Can Denver’s offense finally find a recipe for success on Sunday? You’ll just have to tune in and find out.

summary: As expected, the Detroit Lions activated safety Brian Branch from the Physically Unable to Perform list and Cade Mays from injured reserve on Saturday. The moves make both players eligible to play Sunday against the Green Bay Packers, and the Lions have indicated both will have significant roles this week. The questionable designation has been […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-NOVEMBER 2: Detroit Lions safety Brian Branch #32 enters the field prior to an NFL football game between the Minnesota Vikings and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, November 2, 2025 (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images As expected, the Detroit Lions activated safety Brian Branch from the Physically Unable to Perform list and Cade Mays from injured reserve on Saturday. The moves make both players eligible to play Sunday against the Green Bay Packers, and the Lions have indicated both will have significant roles this week. The questionable designation has been removed from their status designations, as well. For Branch, it’s his first game action since suffering a torn Achilles in early December. The Lions’ defense has struggled immensely without him on the field, particularly in the secondary. Earlier in the week, Lions coach Dan Campbell expressed how much of a difference he can make out there. “Here’s what’s great about getting BB back: BB gives you the flexibility—what do you want to do with anybody else?” Campbell said. “Because there are things you’re going to want to do with BB high, let him play top-down, and then there are things you want him to play underneath. And that doesn’t require somebody else playing off of him necessarily. He’ll make it right.” It’s unclear how much Branch will play against the Packers, but Campbell indicated Friday that they are going to “let him go here and we’ll be smart.” As for Mays, he’ll make his Lions debut on Sunday after the team acquired him on a three-year, $25 million free-agent deal. Mays broke his wrist in training camp, forcing Detroit to rely on Juice Scruggs to be their starting center for the first five games. While Scruggs played well, Campbell indicated that they plan on putting Mays back in the lineup this week. “We really worked the heck out of Cade yesterday. He got some quality reps, and we would like to give him a go here,” Campbell said Wednesday. “… We’d like to just rip this Band-Aid off of Cade. I thought he had some good work yesterday. I thought he looked pretty good.” The Lions did not make any additional moves on Saturday, meaning there are no elevations from the practice squad this week.

title: Green Bay Packers vs. Detroit Lions preview: 5 key stats
summary: The Detroit Lions finally enter the divisional portion of their schedule, looking for redemption after finishing last in the NFC North with a corresponding lowly 2-4 division record last season. That included getting swept by Matt LaFleur’s Green Bay Packers on two notably big stages, in Week 1 and again on Thanksgiving. That came after […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 23: Detroit Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson (97), left, and Detroit Lions safety Tracy Walker III (21), center, sack Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love (10), right, during a traditional Thanksgiving Day NFL football game between the Green Bay Packers and the Detroit Lions on November 23, 2023 at Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Detroit Lions finally enter the divisional portion of their schedule, looking for redemption after finishing last in the NFC North with a corresponding lowly 2-4 division record last season. That included getting swept by Matt LaFleur’s Green Bay Packers on two notably big stages, in Week 1 and again on Thanksgiving. That came after Dan Campbell’s Lions squads had ripped off a 6-1 run against the Packers dating back to late 2021, bridging their dominance over the tail end of Aaron Rodgers’ tenure and the beginning of Jordan Love’s reign. The Lions’ inconsistencies from 2025 have followed them into 2026, as they still haven’t won consecutive games since Weeks 4-5 last year. Now coming off a bye week, they’ve been equally inconsistent following the break under Campbell, posting a 2-2-1 record that includes last season’s embarrassing performance against the Vikings. They’ve averaged 41 points per game in their post-bye victories but mustered just 14.3 points per game in non-victories. Meanwhile, Green Bay’s early-season struggles had them getting churned into cheese curds behind a particularly leaky offensive line, but two impressive wins against the Bears and Cowboys have the Packers heating up at the wrong time for Detroit. This is the time of year when teams tinker, find solutions, and position themselves for a postseason run, separating themselves from the pack. The Lions have a real opportunity to get into the driver’s seat and prove they’re still the team that went 15-3 in the NFC North from 2022-24. Week 7’s return to Ford Field will present the biggest litmus test yet this season for the state of the franchise. After stepping up to the occasion against the Cardinals, it’s time for the Lions to rise to the challenge of a heavyweight bout against the Packers. This week’s preview will examine five key stats and matchups Detroit needs to control to prove itself. Note: Unless otherwise indicated, all statistics are sourced from NFL Pro, FTN Fantasy, Pro Football Reference, SumerSports, or Pro Football Focus. Love Is in the Air The Packers’ and Jordan Love’s reliance on aerial bombardment, along with the classic Packers tendency to draw defensive pass interference penalties, has been well documented as of late. And there’s a justifiable fear factor when considering how often the Lions defense has been lit up like it’s Independence Day this season. A big component of this big-game hunting approach has been the Packers’ offseason decluttering of their wide receiver room, letting Romeo Doubs leave in free agency and trading away Dontayvion Wicks to allow for more consistent usage and development of recently extended Christian Watson and 2025 first-rounder Matthew Golden, two players adept at taking the top off defenses. This season, Golden (42.2%, 8th) and Watson (32.6%, 21st) both rank in the NFL’s top 21 in air yards share rate. Together, they account for 74.8% of Love’s total intended air yards. Their ability to stretch the Lions’ defense downfield is a genuine threat, even with the return of Brian Branch and the development of Keith Abney II at safety. What the Lions defense needs to be particularly careful about is getting shredded by play action when bringing defenders closer to the box and getting caught in single-high shells. Packers receivers on deep passes (20+ air yards) off play action vs. single-high shells: Matthew Golden: 3 targets, 2 receptions, 86 receiving yards Tucker Kraft: 2 targets, 2 receptions, 76 receiving yards Golden (2nd) and Kraft (3rd) both rank among the NFL’s top three in receiving yards on deep play-action passes against single-high defenses, with three of those four catches coming in Week 5 against the Bears. It’s also noteworthy that Watson has two deep-ball catches for 73 receiving yards and a touchdown against single-high shells (without play action), along with another two deep-ball catches for 85 receiving yards and a touchdown off play action (against coverages other than single-high). Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard needs to calibrate his defensive game plan to account for Green Bay’s vertical passing attack, keeping two defenders deep to maintain a lid on the Packers’ offense and avoid getting burned by deep shots off play action. Doing so would go a long way toward giving Detroit a fighting chance. Love Is Blind(side) Building off the Packers’ deep passing attack, while Love ranks third in the league with 12 deep-pass completions and second with 453 deep passing yards, he’s been somewhat inconsistent in that department. His 35.3% completion percentage on deep passes ranks just 23rd, directly behind Deshaun Watson and Bo Nix, while seven of his completions (1st) and 279 of his deep passing yards (1st) have come in Weeks 5-6 alone. That brings us to the two sides of the Packers’ offensive coin: Have they found their rhythm and some answers, or did they simply find success against the Bears’ and Cowboys’ defenses? Not that the Lions’ defense has been any better than those two, but Detroit might have an avenue to disrupt some of Green Bay’s recent passing success. When comparing how opposing pass rushes attacked Jordan Love in Weeks 1-4 versus Weeks 5-6, we actually see that Love faced slightly higher quarterback pressure and sack rates while enjoying considerably more success over the last two weeks. However, that doesn’t tell the whole story. From Weeks 1-4, the collective defenses of the Vikings, Jets, Falcons, and Buccaneers forced Love into an average time to throw of 2.15 seconds (1st, fastest), while generating pressure in an average of 1.86 seconds (3rd-fastest) and blitzing him on 40.7% of dropbacks (3rd-most). Compare that to Weeks 5-6, when Love’s average time to throw increased to 2.49 seconds (13th), his average time to pressure climbed to a more comfortable 2.24 seconds (t-14th), and the blitz rate dipped to 31.6% (19th). Jordan Love vs. Pressure | Weeks 1-4 vs. Weeks 5-6 Weeks 1-4: 51.3 passer rating (23rd), 40.5% completion percentage (19th), 6.4 yards/attempt (16th), -0.424 EPA/dropback (22nd), 35.1% success rate (19th), 10.8% explosive play rate (14th) Weeks 5-6: 97.0 passer rating (5th), 61.1% completion percentage (6th), 10.6 yards/attempt (3rd), +0.293 EPA/dropback (3rd), 61.1% success rate (3rd), 22.2% explosive play rate (3rd) Jordan Love vs. Blitz | Weeks 1-4 vs. Weeks 5-6 Weeks 1-4: 89.0 passer rating (21st), 53.2% completion percentage (33rd), 7.0 yards/attempt (20th), -0.236 EPA/dropback (28th), 40.3% success rate (27th), 11.3% explosive play rate (t-13th) Weeks 5-6: 113.5 passer rating (6th), 66.7% completion percentage (9th), 10.1 yards/attempt (5th), +0.403 EPA/dropback (3rd), 58.3% success rate (8th), 20.8% explosive play rate (2nd) The sample size is small, but it’s undeniable that Love and the Packers’ offense have shown a night-and-day difference in their ability to handle pressure and the blitz over the last two weeks. Some of that improvement could be attributed to a more settled offensive line, with Jordan Morgan, Laken Tomlinson, Sean Rhyan, Travis Glover, and Anthony Belton entrenched as the starters from left to right over the last three weeks, providing additional competence and stability after Green Bay shuffled through several combinations in Weeks 1-3. Even then, the Packers could look to start Aaron Banks, who has been practicing this week, at left guard and Kevin Zeitler, who was active last week, at right guard. It’s all up in the air, but what’s not in question is that Love has looked more…

title: Lions vs. Packers 5 Qs preview: Unpacking Jordan Love’s volatile numbers
summary: Fresh off their early-season bye, the Detroit Lions pick up where they left off against their first NFC North opponent: the Green Bay Packers. We had the pleasure of connecting with Justis Mosqueda, the Team Community Producer for Acme Packing Company, to give us some insight into this Packers team ahead of this week’s matchup. […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 27: Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers prepares to throw during an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on November 27, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Fresh off their early-season bye, the Detroit Lions pick up where they left off against their first NFC North opponent: the Green Bay Packers. We had the pleasure of connecting with Justis Mosqueda, the Team Community Producer for Acme Packing Company , to give us some insight into this Packers team ahead of this week’s matchup. We learned about Jordan Love’s wild mix of quick releases and deep shots amidst Green Bay’s pass-protection woes, the ongoing O-line carousel and Josh Jacobs’ potential impact on the run game, as well as Jonathan Gannon’s hyper-aggressive blitz scheme—plus much more. 1. Jordan Love’s numbers are the most fascinating thing to unpack with this Packers offense. He has the shortest time to throw in the NFL among 37 qualifying quarterbacks (2.48 seconds), yet he sports the sixth-highest average depth of target (9.5 yards) and according to Pro Football Focus, leads the league in big-time throws (15) and passing attempts of 20+ yards downfield (33). Through six weeks of the season, what’s the story of Love between these numbers? In short: Heroics. The offensive line performed poorly in the pass-protection game outside of Weeks 4 and 5. He has absolutely no running game to speak of. Love is taking a massive pounding week to week. It really is just the Kobe stan in Love coming out and willing the team to victory. The team also leads the NFL in drops over this time period, too, and a lot of those are on what would have been explosives and/or touchdowns. It’s incredibly frustrating to watch Love play at such a high level with the rest of the offense playing poorly around him. 2. Likely associated with Love’s performance this season is the offensive line and the running game. Injuries have thrown Green Bay’s offensive line into the centrifuge. Since the start of the season, they’ve acquired some familiar faces in Laken Tomlinson and Kevin Zeitler, and they’ve done their fair share of shuffling to figure out the best combination. Is this the week Zeitler makes his season debut? What’s your level of confidence in this line solidifying itself by the time these two teams meet again in January? Meanwhile, the Packers have one of the worst rushing attacks in the league–but Josh Jacobs did come off the Commissioner’s Exempt List on Monday. How much do you anticipate Jacobs playing in this game based on Matt LaFleur’s comments this week, and do you think he’s the kind of difference maker who can single handedly get this run game out of the basement? I really think it could be. The running game has been bad all year, but at least Week 4 and 5 were games where the offensive line could at least protect Love. Last week, the Packers went into five-man protections for most of the game for the first time all season. This ended up exposing both guards a little more than anyone seemed to expect (Jacob Monk and Donovan Jennings started the year at guard before the team transitioned to Travis Glover and Laken Tomlinson). As of Thursday’s practice, the Packers were repping seven players to get ready for this game: the starting center (Sean Rhyan), the two tackles (Anthony Belton and Jordan Morgan) and four guard options (Glover, Tomlinson, Aaron Banks and Kevin Zeitler). I would not be shocked at all if we get Banks at left guard and Zeitler at right guard this week. If the Packers want to make that change before Week 9, they kind of have to do it now, because they have a short week against the Carolina Panthers after this. I 100 percent think Jacobs is going to play this week. LaFleur has really backed him at every opportunity to do so. The team has very much been in the business of getting Jacobs back on the field, even prior to the legal process playing out. They said he’s been working out with the team and in meetings the entire time. He just hasn’t been able to practice with them. They have three open roster spots on the 53-man roster that they’re keeping open right now, and two of those (Jacobs and PUP player Jordan Riley) are probably already filled in their minds. I think Jacobs can help turn some of those -2 runs into +2 runs, but I don’t think he’s just going to come into the lineup and fix all of Green Bay’s running game issues himself. 3. Former defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley left for a head coaching gig with the Miami Dolphins, and the Packers brought in Jonathan Gannon to replace him. What are some of the most notable differences you’ve noticed between the two coordinators, have said differences been mostly positive, negative or somewhere in between, and do you feel like the eventual return of Micah Parsons will end up making all the difference? The Hafley scheme was interesting, because it was mostly a scheme that disguised coverages, but didn’t do much on the pressure end, up until Micah Parsons came to town. When Parsons was on the field, teams obviously adjusted and ended up playing the Packers in more quick game and run game situations, which really forced Hafley to play more bland schemes—and Hafley went back to some “hidden” coverages once Parsons went down with an injury. Gannon’s defense really has been about bringing pressure. He’ll send seven guys on the first play of the game without blinking, and the cornerbacks have been playing pretty well this year (all three safeties have been great). They’ve done some interesting things with individual teams’ pass-blocking rules to get free rushers. It’s not uncommon for Gannon to scheme up a pressure where there are seven blockers on four rushers, one of the rushers is a free rusher, and the Packers still have seven coverage players for just three route-runners. The only time the defense hasn’t looked elite was against the Atlanta Falcons, which was a weird game. Bijan Robinson went crazy, and it seemed like everyone on both sides of the ball were slipping on the field that night other than Robinson. I think a lot of people are wondering if that was just a one-off or what the Packers’ defense looks like against a dynamic back. I think this week’s matchup will sort of answer that for us. Hopefully, Micah Parsons will be a big addition down the line, yes. Please, God. 4. Green Bay lost Edgerrin Cooper for the season after he suffered a torn Achilles in Week 4. Who has Gannon called on to replace Cooper, and how have the Packers adjusted on defense since the injury? Have you noticed any shifting in personnel groupings/deployment without their star linebacker available? EDITOR’S NOTE: This was asked and answered before Zaire Franklin suffered a mid-week injury and was declared out. The Packers use their linebackers a lot on special teams, because LaFleur’s offensive players hardly play teams—outside of the return positions. So they have Zaire Franklin at the Mike position (he doesn’t play teams) and now the Will role (previously Cooper) is being split by Isaiah McDuffie and Ty’Ron Hopper. My guess is they’re rotating McDuffie and Hopper (they change every two series or so) so that they can keep their legs fresh on special teams. Behind them, Green Bay rosters two linebackers who are functionally special teams-only players in Nick Niemann and Kristian Welch, if you want to know how important those linebackers are for the Packers’ special teams unit. Last week, they also called up Arron Mosby (a hybrid edge-linebacker who is basically another full-time special teamer) against the Cowboys. Both McDuffie and Hopper have played well, but the linebackers have never really been tested (outside of the run game against Atlanta) this entire season. No one is really throwing over the middle against us, in part because we’re sending blitzers so much. It’s sort of hard to evaluate the position right now. In the moments when you would expect…

title: What should become a Detroit Lions tradition at Ford Field?
summary: If you visit football stadiums around the country, you will notice that most everyone has their own thing. From the University of Michigan’s singing of “Mr. Brightside” to the way the Kansas City Chiefs cap off the singing of the national anthem, almost everyone has a unique flair to their gameday presentation. full_text: If you visit football stadiums around the country, you will notice that most everyone has their own thing. From the University of Michigan’s singing of “Mr. Brightside” to the way the Kansas City Chiefs cap off the singing of the national anthem, almost everyone has a unique flair to their gameday presentation. And that is no different for the Detroit Lions, as Ford Field has consistently been one of the toughest places for opponents to play. One of the biggest additions has been the arrival of the Lions stadium DJ, Djrayyadig , who does an amazing job of incorporating both modern and old-school Detroit-centric hits, especially during pre-game warmups. Then there is the massive presence of Theo Gridiron Spight . From leading the singing of “Gridiron Heroes” after the Lions score, to his countdown that gets the crowd amped up just before kickoff. Overall, the Lions’ gameday presentation at Ford Field is S-tier stuff. However, one thing that came up recently when talking to a friend is the fact that we don’t have anything that specifically signifies the start of the fourth quarter. That brings us to today’s question of the day—what fourth quarter tradition would you want incorporated into gamedays? My answer: I would go with something along the lines of a song that gets the players and fans going as the game turns to the fourth and final quarter. It could be the same song week-to-week, or it could be a rotation of tracks from Detroit’s history. One of the first that comes to mind is Tee Grizzley’s “ First Day Out, ” or Trick Trick and Eminem’s, “ Welcome to Detroit .” If we wanted to keep it old school, it could be a timeless, legendary classic like Marvin Gaye’s “Trouble Man.” I think this would be a great way to pay homage to the city while also getting the crowd ready for the fourth quarter. What do you think? What kind of fourth quarter or in-game tradition would you want implemented at Ford Field? Let us know in the comments below. Join the conversation! title: If Josh Jacobs performs only as expected, the Packers’ rushing game will improve
summary: All signs are pointing to Josh Jacobs returning to the lineup this weekend. Your mileage may vary on whether or not you think he should, based on the legal situation he faced this year and the still-looming question of whether or not a potentially damaging video will come out, but it seems inarguable that his […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - DECEMBER 20: Josh Jacobs #8 of the Green Bay Packers runs the ball during the second half of an NFL football game against the Chicago Bears at Solider Field on December 20, 2025 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images All signs are pointing to Josh Jacobs returning to the lineup this weekend. Your mileage may vary on whether or not you think he should, based on the legal situation he faced this year and the still-looming question of whether or not a potentially damaging video will come out, but it seems inarguable that his return will help the Packers’ backfield. We’ve written again and again about how bad the Packers’ rushing attack has been this year. Bad might not even be the best word to use anymore. Embarrassing might be better. The Packers are a distant 32nd in total rushing yards this season, having managed just 359 so far this year. But Jacobs’ return can help! As the Packers play out a one-team experiment on whether or not running backs matter, Jacobs can help the situation by doing the one thing the Packers’ backs haven’t been able to do this year: perform as expected. Rushing Yards Over Expected (RYOE) is one of the most interesting advanced stats out there right now, and it doesn’t paint the Packers in a particularly flattering light. T he product of the 2020 Big Data Bowl , RYOE uses historical datasets to calculate how many yards a ballcarrier should be expected to gain in a given down and distance from a given spot on the field. So far this year, the Packers’ non-quarterback ballcarriers have produced the staggering total of -116 RYOE. MarShawn Lloyd alone accounts -75. Chris Brooks leads the team with a grand total of one (1) RYOE. It’s been bad! If you wiped out the Packers’ negative RYOE, their running game would see an immediate and drastic improvement. An additional 116 yards would bump the Packers from dead last in the league to a tie for 29th. Put differently, if the Packers ballcarriers produced only as expected and no better, they’d make a quick move away from being the worst running game in the league. Jacobs, at the very least, should be able to do that. An inside grinder who’s never been particularly big or fast, Jacobs has made his living as a runner hitting the designed hole hard and correctly. Even allowing for how poor the Packers’ run blocking has been this year, and it’s been bad, there have been plenty of plays where a Packers running back simply has failed to go where he’s supposed to. To say nothing of what he could offer as a receiver or a pass blocker, Jacobs should at least be able to go where he’s supposed to go. If he can at least be a net neutral on the ground, gaining only what he’s expect to get and nothing more, he’ll represent a significant and dramatic improvement for the Packers’ rushing game.

title: To survive Detroit shootout, Packers should look to Thanksgiving win
summary: It’s no secret the Packers game against the Detroit Lions on Sunday is likely to be a shootout. As a byproduct of their stellar offense and inability to slow anyone on defense, Detroit hasn’t played a low-scoring game all year. In every Lions game so far this season, both teams have scored at least 21 […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 27: Dontayvion Wicks #13 of the Green Bay Packers scores a touchdown against Thomas Harper #12 of the Detroit Lions during the second quarter at Ford Field on November 27, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s no secret the Packers game against the Detroit Lions on Sunday is likely to be a shootout. As a byproduct of their stellar offense and inability to slow anyone on defense, Detroit hasn’t played a low-scoring game all year. In every Lions game so far this season, both teams have scored at least 21 points. In four of the five, both teams have scored at least 24. In two, both teams scored at least 30. If you like offense, you’ll probably like watching the Detroit Lions play football. The Packers, meanwhile, haven’t really been in a high scoring game this year. The Packers have only broken 30 once, and both times their opponents have done it, the Packers haven’t seemed super interested in keeping pace. Obviously they’ll have to avoid that outcome if they want a chance against the Lions. Fortunately, there’s a recent example of how the Packers should approach a game likely to result in a high-scoring shootout: their Thanksgiving day showdown with the Lions last year. That game alone should have showed the Packers exactly the kind of aggressive, playmaker-focused game they’ll need to play to beat the Lions this week. It starts with fourth down conversions. Matt LaFleur has trended back towards aggressiveness on fourth downs this year, and his choices against the Lions last November shows how that approach can pay off. The Packers converted all three fourth down tries last year, scoring two touchdowns (a 27-yard strike to Dontayvion Wicks and a one-yard score by Romeo Doubs) and putting the game away on their final drive. The third conversion deserves special attention. Facing a 4th and 3 on the Lions’ 45-yard line with just under two minutes to go, the Packers made the high-risk, high-reward decision to go for it. Given that the Lions had no timeouts, a conversion would end the game. But throw incomplete or come up short, and the Lions would have been in business, needing less than 20 yards to get into field goal range. Matt LaFleur put the ball in Jordan Love’s hands, and Love delivered, finding Wicks for a 16-yard completion. That sort of approach should again pay dividends against the Lions, who you can expect to be aggressive whenever they have the ball as well. The Packers’ aggressiveness should also extend to their playcalling. Last year, LaFleur and Love went deep often. Seven of Love’s 30 passing attempts that day were to targets more than 20 yards downfield. He completed four of those seven targets for 126 yards and two touchdowns. That’s not quite as good as Love’s heat check performance against the Bears, but it’s close enough,and considering how poor the Lions’ passing defense is by virtually every measure (in or near the bottom quarter in almost every stat you can find), I think we can reasonably assume he’ll have a chance to move the ball against the Lions this week. They should take advantage. They’ll need some defensive plays, though. Last year, Micah Parsons brought plenty. He came up with three sacks, two of which were on third down. On a second half third down, the Lions were lined up on the Packers’ four-yard line, trailing by 10. Parsons broke through and took down Jared Goff for a nine-yard loss, and the Lions kicked a field goal. If not for the sack, would Detroit have attempted a field goal or gone for it all? We’ll never know, but Parsons’ sack definitely changed the calculus. Parsons obviously won’t be on the field this week, but the need for playmaking is no less important, especially with Zaire Franklin on the sideline. Defensive stops may not forestall a shootout entirely, but a few crucial big plays could tilt the field. Looking to the past is no guarantee of success. The Packers have certainly changed quite a bit since last Thanksgiving. But the lessons learned in that widely watched game are still relevant today, and if the Packers can run the same script, they’ll be in great shape.

full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images This is not a headlining week of college football, as there are only two top-25 matchups in the sport, but as we saw in Week 7, when the sport got turned upside down, sometimes the more interesting games are upsets, not big brands playing against each other head-to-head. This is going to be an open thread for all of you to discuss Saturday’s college football action, including if you’re watching games for a 2027 NFL draft perspective. We’ll break down the top-25 matchups, including who the projected top-100 selections are on each team, according to the current consensus board. #7 Mississippi @ #19 Texas – 6:30 pm CT, ABC #2: Colin Simmons, ED, Texas (out) #5: Arch Manning, QB, Texas #10: Trevor Goosby, OL, Texas #12: Trinidad Chambliss, QB, Mississippi #13: Cam Coleman, WR, Texas #15: Will Echoles, DL, Mississippi #49: Melvin Siani, OL, Texas #53: Kewan Lacy, RB, Mississippi #54: Deuce Alexander, WR, Mississippi #63: Ryan Wingo, WR, Texas #64: Jelani McDonald, S, Texas #74: Rasheem Biles, LB, Texas The best player in this game should have been edge rusher Colin Simmons, who has some Micah Parsons in his game, but Simmons will be out with a high ankle sprain that will continue to cost him games down the stretch. The headliners here are obviously quarterbacks Arch Manning and Trinidad Chambliss, who are sort of moving in opposite directions. Coming into the year, the expectation was that Manning was going to be the top draft prospect in this class. Now, he’s already been jumped by Oklahoma State’s Drew Mestemaker at the quarterback position, and Miami’s Darian Mensah, Notre Dame’s CJ Carr and Chambliss, who is currently third in the Heisman odds behind Ohio State receiver Jeremiah Smith and Mensah, are breathing down Manning’s neck. Texas is probably one loss away from being on real shaky ground for the college football playoff. This is going to be a huge game for both sides. #14 Houston @ #10 Utah – 9:15 pm CT, ESPN #37: Zereoue Williams, OL, Utah #93: Anthony Boswell, OL, Houston There’s not a lot of top-end talent in this game, but Utah tackle Zereoue Williams is a huge riser this season. He wasn’t really on the draft radar for many teams, as he only played 156 snaps in 2025 after a season-ending injury in 2024, but the 6’8” tackle is now getting some first-round buzz. Maybe he’s a tackle prospect who could be around for the Packers’ first pick of the 2027 draft, a second-round selection. While he didn’t make the cut as a “top-100” prospect, Conner Weigman is currently listed as the #103 player in the class on the consensus board. The Houston quarterback has been putting up video-game numbers (15 touchdowns, 1 interception) this season, and the Texas A&M transfer looks like he has an NFL future. title: No Colts player reportedly ‘off-limits’ if rebuild begins before upcoming trade deadline
summary: According to NFL Insider Tom Pelissero, no Indianapolis Colts player is considered “off-limits,” should the franchise choose to be major sellers ahead of the league’s upcoming Tuesday, November 10th, trade deadline and jumpstart what seems like an inevitable major rebuild regardless: “The Colts have received strong trade interest in guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - OCTOBER 12: Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor (28) runs behind Indianapolis Colts guard Quenton Nelson (56) during and NFL game between the Indianapolis Colts and the Arizona Cardinals on October 12, 2025 at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, IN (Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images According to NFL Insider Tom Pelissero, no Indianapolis Colts player is considered “off-limits,” should the franchise choose to be major sellers ahead of the league’s upcoming Tuesday, November 10th, trade deadline and jumpstart what seems like an inevitable major rebuild regardless: “The Colts have received strong trade interest in guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner in recent days, and no player is expected to be off-limits—if they decide to sell before the November 10 trade deadline,” writes Pelissero on his substack ‘The Sweep’ . “That includes running back Jonathan Taylor, who also figures to be the subject of calls over the next couple of weeks.” Still, the consensus among league insiders seems to be that team ownership, and namely Carlie Irsay-Gordon, want to give embattled head coach Shane Steichen and this team two more weeks to see if they can rite the ship, and who knows, maybe the firing of longtime general manager Chris Ballard can help galvanize the team a bit. That being said, the looming schedule ahead of the league’s trade deadline isn’t exactly encouraging, with a road matchup against the undefeated Minnesota Vikings (5-0), as well as the AFC South leading Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2) thereafter, a road environment where Indianapolis hasn’t won since 2014. In my opinion, it makes sense ( although still initially painful! ) to rip off the Bandaid and trade veteran players such as DeForest Buckner (32) and Grover Stewart (33), who realistically don’t fit into a 2-3 year rebuild timeline ( *if hopefully done well by the Colts next general manager* ), and that is, if the Colts can get meaningful future draft capital in return respectively. For instance, acquiring a second round pick for Buckner and a fourth rounder for Stewart from an NFL suitor would be ideal going forward. Even trading veteran cornerback Charvarius Ward (30) for any value in return probably makes some sense, if he doesn’t factor into the Colts plans beyond the 2026 season. The Colts would probably be more hard-pressed to trade the homegrown pairing of offensive guard Quenton Nelson or running back Jonathan Taylor without getting at least a future first round pick in return for either future franchise Ring of Honor candidate and potential Pro Football Hall of Famer. In particular, Nelson, given his impeccable technique and fundamentals, may age rather gracefully into his mid-thirties like other elite offensive guards at his position historically—even when his athleticism and playing strength diminish a bit due to father time and added wear-and-tear. Still, Indianapolis doesn’t have a 2027 first round pick due to last year’s Sauce Gardner trade deadline deal, meaning they may be a little more motivated to get that type of ‘Day 1’ pick back than they ordinarily would. At any rate, it’s a situation well worth monitoring over the next two weeks or so.

title: Colts make roster moves ahead of road matchup vs. Minnesota
summary: On Saturday, the Indianapolis Colts announced that veteran linebacker Germaine Pratt has been elevated to the practice squad, along with cornerback Kenneth Harris just ahead of their Week 7 road matchup against the Minnesota Vikings. Regarding Pratt, it comes after rookie linebacker CJ Allen (ankle) has been downgraded to out for Sunday, with fellow rookie […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - DECEMBER 28: Germaine Pratt #53 of the Indianapolis Colts reacts after a touchdown during the game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Lucas Oil Stadium on December 28, 2025 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Hickey/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Saturday, the Indianapolis Colts announced that veteran linebacker Germaine Pratt has been elevated to the practice squad, along with cornerback Kenneth Harris just ahead of their Week 7 road matchup against the Minnesota Vikings. Regarding Pratt, it comes after rookie linebacker CJ Allen (ankle) has been downgraded to out for Sunday, with fellow rookie linebacker Bryce Boettcher (groin) still questionable. The 30-year-old Pratt was signed to the Colts practice squad a little less than two weeks ago, after somewhat surprisingly remaining unsigned as a veteran free agent all offseason. After being released by the Las Vegas Raiders after the first 4 starts in 2025, Pratt was quickly signed by the Colts, where he recorded 101 tackles (57 solo), an interception, 8 passes defensed, a forced fumble, and 2 fumble recoveries during 12 ensuing starts with Indianapolis last year. To his credit, Pratt actually helped shore up some of the Colts early lackluster starting linebacker play and was actually a positive in run defense, even if he’s conversely, a bit slow of foot in pass coverage. Given the Colts recent injuries and rather underwhelming play at the starting linebacker position again, Pratt was recently signed as veteran insurance and has rejoined Colts defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo yet again. The pairing dates back to their days together in Cincinnati defensively. It wouldn’t be surprising to see Pratt play a pivotal role again for the Colts this season. Meanwhile, Colts punter Rigoberto Sanchez (right foot), who sustained a big hit during a blocked punt in last Sunday’s brutal loss, will be available in Minnesota—as Indianapolis cut ties with grizzled veteran punter Thomas Morstead from their practice squad, who was signed as another veteran insurance policy earlier in the week. The 24-year-old Harris, who was originally signed by the New England Patriots as an undrafted rookie free agent earlier this past offseason, has appeared in 1 game for Indianapolis so far this season, recording a single tackle.

title: Long awaited move starts Colts in new direction?
summary: Let me start by saying that although I have supported Ballard longer than most, I’m not shocked or disappointed by the announcement of his firing. It wouldn’t have surprised me two years ago, I endorsed it last year, and completely agreed with the mandate accompanying his retention this year. My main complaint is different than […]
full_text: Let me start by saying that although I have supported Ballard longer than most, I’m not shocked or disappointed by the announcement of his firing. It wouldn’t have surprised me two years ago, I endorsed it last year, and completely agreed with the mandate accompanying his retention this year. My main complaint is different than most, in that I think his inability to find the right coach(s) has been the worst aspect of his tenure. I think it outweighs the QB carousel and DE draft misses, but all three contributed to his demise. Now, how am I supposed to feel better about the team than I did before the dismissal? This is where I struggle. I don’t think that removing Ballard lifts some Pig Pen cloud above the Colts headquarters. So, if my goal is to feel better about the Colts chances this year, where do I find that spark? The roster will make changes that likely only lessens the talent level for this years team, at least if you believe reports of a fire sale, with anyone in a contract year being available. We also appear willing to let Lou and Shane continue to call the shots, which doesn’t do much for my search of that spark. I’m not willing to say that we should just suck for a couple of years, then start winning championships. My memory of the first 15 years here in Indy are more about the fun I had before and after the game, than much of the product on the field. We were the Dolts and along with some of the mediocre seasons that we seem to hate, came more god awful results than, well, nearly everyone else in the league. Cheering at the game was usually reserved for the first quarter. I often was able to move from upper level seats to pretty much wherever I wanted to sit. I’m painting a bleak picture, but that is how it was. So how do I manage to stay my optimistic self, with the fact that this season looks to resemble one of the first 15? Losing is suppose to be the springboard to better things. As bad as some of those seasons were, I don’t think I ever had the “pack it in” feeling by week 6, as I do this year. Here are things that we can expect to see the rest of this year. With two lame-duck coaches, what can we expect from the players? Will they “ball out” for Ed Dodds, thinking that he will have any say on who stays or goes this year and beyond? There will always be a level of professionalism from many players, but being a little dinged up will turn into being out, maybe even to the IR. Those on IR, are not likely to return, as why risk it? Have you checked out the practice reports for this week? Muscle memory will take care of me watching the game. I will still avoid the media as to keep the results of our game a mystery, until it is available for my streaming after the game. I will still have a couple of cold ones and don a jersey of either blue or white, whichever color we are in that game day. I’ll still watch and think we have a chance, I just don’t know how far into the game that will last? I hope that fast forward does not become too much of a part of my game watching experience. The good news about being an optimist, is that it wont take much for me to start seeing our glass as half full. Maybe the D starts to gel as young players find their stride? Maybe the O-line steps up from okayish, to pretty good, allowing the offense to do as some of us envisioned? What if Burks can be player to be counted on? I think all three can happen, so there has to be at some optimism left in here somewhere. I really do not want to wait until next year for it to re-emerge, but I think this season is going to test it.

title: Let’s Argue: Chiefs need to improve or will go .500 the rest of the way
summary: In our “Let’s Argue” series, Mark Gunnels considers the hot takes, wacky predictions and unpopular opinions of Kansas City Chiefs fans from all over the world. 5crawfishdinners says: If our average level of play doesn’t improve over the first five games, we’ll go .500 over the last 12 games I disagree because one thing we’ve […]
full_text: (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images In our “Let’s Argue” series, Mark Gunnels considers the hot takes, wacky predictions and unpopular opinions of Kansas City Chiefs fans from all over the world. 5crawfishdinners says: If our average level of play doesn’t improve over the first five games, we’ll go .500 over the last 12 games I disagree because one thing we’ve learned about the Chiefs over the years is that they tend to play down to their competition, but they also know how to elevate their game when the stakes are higher. You can’t just look at their average level of play and assume that’s what you’ll get every week, especially against the better teams in the league. This team has consistently shown it can flip that switch when it matters most. bgack says: Chiefs win Super Bowl over the 49ers I can definitely see Chiefs-49ers Part 3 in the Super Bowl. These are arguably the two most complete teams in football, and both have the coaching, talent, and experience to make another deep postseason run. But until San Francisco proves it can beat Mahomes when it matters most, I’m rolling with Kansas City AGAIN. aadicker says: The Chiefs’ first loss of the season will be against the Falcons I agree the Buffalo Bills are the biggest threat because Josh Allen will always make them dangerous, especially in January. But I’m not sleeping on the Jacksonville Jaguars either — they’ve got enough talent on both sides of the ball to be a real problem in the AFC. That said, if the Chiefs get to the postseason healthy with Mahomes, an improved running game, and a defense that keeps developing, I’ll take my chances against anybody. CleverlyNamed says: We do not need another WR and trading for one midseason will not move the needle much I disagree because while I don’t think the Chiefs necessarily NEED another receiver, that doesn’t mean adding the right guy wouldn’t move the needle. If a legitimate difference-maker becomes available, why wouldn’t you explore it, especially when you’re trying to maximize another Super Bowl window with Patrick Mahomes? There’s a big difference between making a move just to make one and adding a weapon who could take this offense to another level.

We have placed RB Brashard Smith on Reserve/Injured. pic.twitter.com/fZX4YNjghi — Kansas City Chiefs (@Chiefs) October 24, 2026 The team is adding a defensive reinforcement in second-year linebacker Cooper McDonald, who has been on the team’s Reserve/Injured (IR) list since leaving Week 1’s contest against the Denver Broncos with a knee injury. The Chiefs designated McDonald to return to practice this week, and he drew a questionable tag on this week’s final injury report . Now that he has been put back on the active roster, the Chiefs removed his game designation for Sunday night. On Friday, head coach Andy Reid confirmed that third string running back Brashard Smith would be listed as out for Sunday due to a hamstring injury and that practice squad rookie Jadyn Ott would make his NFL debut in his place. That will apparently be the status for the next month. Rather than a practice squad elevation, Ott has been signed to the 53-man roster with Smith heading to IR. Smith will be out for at least Kansas City’s next four games. Veteran wide receiver Justin Watson did receive a practice squad call up for this week’s contest. Watson returned to the Chiefs earlier this month, where he played from 2022-24. He signed to the practice squad in the wake of injuries to wideouts Tyquan Thornton and Rashee Rice. Thorton is likely out for the season after dislocating his ankle in Week 4. Rice will miss his second consecutive contest on Sunday with a hamstring injury. Watson — who was released by the Houston Texans before the season — was elevated in Week 6 to suit up against the Los Angeles Chargers . He played only one offensive snap in his season debut and did not see a target. He also played three special teams snaps. title: Chiefs-Seahawks: 5 questions with Field Gulls ahead of Week 7
summary: On Sunday, the Kansas City Chiefs face the Seattle Seahawks in a Sunday night lights of Week 7 games. We welcome John Gilbert of Field Gulls — our sister SBNation site covering the Seahawks— for Five Questions with the Enemy. Download the SB Nation app on your mobile device and join the Field Gulls community […]
full_text: (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Sunday, the Kansas City Chiefs face the Seattle Seahawks in a Sunday night lights of Week 7 games. We welcome John Gilbert of Field Gulls — our sister SBNation site covering the Seahawks— for Five Questions with the Enemy . Chiefs Kingdom, bring the noise to the SB Nation app! Join fellow Chiefs fans to react to every explosive play and game-changing moment in real time. Chat live throughout the game Browse with fewer ads Easily jump between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Download the SB Nation app on your mobile device and join the Field Gulls community through Sunday’s game to get perspectives from both sides of the Week 7 matchup! 1. The Seahawks are 3-3 after losing three of their last four games, with all three losses coming by three points or fewer. They also committed 10 turnovers in those three losses. What has been the biggest reason the defending Super Bowl champions have struggled to close out games this season? You hit the nail on the head with the turnovers. The Commanders had touchdown drives of 21 and 43 yards, along with a pick six, while the 49ers had touchdown drives of 18 yard and 11 yards to go along with a defensive touchdown when the Seahawks fumbled in their own end zone. In spite of all the issues with turnovers during the four stretch, the game was tied or the Seahawks held the lead in the fourth quarter of all three losses. However, instead of closing out the game like the 2025 squad would have, they have been unable to put the ball in the end zone when needed in high leverage situations. 2. Sam Darnold has thrown seven touchdowns and seven interceptions, including four interceptions during Seattle’s current two-game losing streak. Mike Macdonald has publicly stated that he is not considering a quarterback change. How confident is Seattle that Darnold can rediscover the form that helped lead the Seahawks to a championship? The $100.5M question since the Seahawks signed Darnold in free agency ahead of the 2025 season was which version of him were they getting. Were they getting the quarterback who threw for 4,153 yards and 35 touchdowns through Week 17, or the one who was sacked eleven times while throwing a single touchdown over the final two games of his Vikings career? The reality is, Darnold is who he is, and he often struggles against pressure. His torrid performance during the first half of the 2025 season was largely driven by Klint Kubiak using a lot of 12 and 13 personnel, which defenses defended by loading the box, which in turn created one on one matchups for receivers with single-high safety looks. Kubiak and Darnold feasted on this, but in Week 11 the Rams showed the league it was far more effective to match the Seattle offense based on down and distance rather than personnel. As a result of that, over the second half of the 2025 season the team played at a high level and won ten games in a row, but the offense sputtered at times as the explosive plays that had propelled the early season success became more rare. That leads to the question of what the difference between the second half of 2025 and the start of 2026 is, and it comes down to several parts. First, Darnold does not look to be moving like he is fully healthy just yet after suffering a glute injury on the fifth snap of the season opener against the Patriots. Add to that an injury to starting right guard Anthony Bradford, combined with the loss of both of the top two running backs from the 2025 season in Zach Charbonnet and Kenneth Walker. Bradford has certainly struggled at times as a pass protector in his career, but he’s a 330 pound guard with a mean streak who can make his presence known as a people mover in the ground game. Losing Walker has certainly hurt and I’ll cover that in more detail in the next question, but not having Charbonnet for the first six weeks has likely had a significant impact on the ability of the team to put points on the board in the red zone. Charbonnet lacks Walker’s explosiveness, but throughout his career he has been a very disciplined runner and has been very effective and productive in the red zone, and they’ve lacked ground production in the red zone as it took until Week 4 before a Seattle running back scored a rushing touchdown this year. 3. Seattle allowed Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III to leave in free agency, and he now returns to Lumen Field with 665 rushing yards and six rushing touchdowns through five games. How does the organization’s decision to move on from Walker look now that the Seahawks have struggled to establish consistency in their backfield? This is a discussion that began before the 2025 season even ended, escalated when Charbonnet was lost to a torn ACL in the postseason and has not really ceased or even slowed in months since. The reality is it was unlikely Walker would be retained due to the market he created for himself with his performance down the stretch and in the postseason. Walker has an undeniable physical skillset, but that skillset did not always translate into consistent on field production, and in every season of his career in Seattle he posted the lowest success rate of all running backs on the roster. Simultaneously, he consistently finished in the bottom half of the league in stuff rate in each of those years, and while he improved every year, the Seahawks apparently weren’t interested in paying market rate for Walker’s services while continuing to show the improvement he demonstrated late in the 2025 season. This was a direct result of Walker’s propensity to try and bounce runs to the outside and then win a foot race to the corner. When he wins that race and turns the corner, it’s routinely a big play, but especially on zone runs he failed to run within the system and follow his reads regularly enough. Interestingly, Klint Kubiak tweaked his playcalling tendencies with Walker, specifically giving Walker the ball on gap runs at a rate higher than he had called for any running back during his career as an offensive coordinator, and then over the course of the season called for Walker to carry the ball behind zone blocking more and more. And now it appears that Andy Reid and Chiefs fans are the beneficiary of that, and so far it’s looking like an absolute home run signing for Kansas City. On the Seattle side, first round pick Jadarian Price landing on injured reserve and Charbonnet spending the first six weeks of the season on the PUP list has only exacerbated the frustration of fans who did not want to see Walker depart. So, while George Holani and Emanuel Wilson haven’t lived up to the high hopes of Seahawks fans, those two were undrafted coming out of college for a reason and Charbonnet returning combined with Darnold protecting the ball better should see the situation improve. 4. Seattle enters this matchup ranked first in the NFL in total defense, allowing only 237 yards per game, and Andy Reid called Mike Macdonald’s unit “the best in the business.” What is the biggest matchup advantage the Seahawks’ defense has against Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs’ offense? The biggest thing a Mike Macdonald defense does is play stout and disciplined against the run, which eventually creates third and long situations where they can create unfavorable matchups for the offense with pressure and/or disguised coverages. At a foundational level it is not all that different from what Steve Spagnuolo likes to do with the Chiefs, just with less blitzing and a little more unpredictability. The Walker storyline adds an extra layer of intrigue, as the last time the Seattle defense allowed an opponent to rush for more than 100 yards was in Week 8 of the 2024 season, while Walker has run for 100 yards in six of his last eight games dating back to the 2025 postseason. It’s a fascinating matchup, and as a fan I’m excited to ee Macdonald and Reid face off against one another. 5. The…

title: Kenneth Walker treating Seattle return ‘like any other week’
summary: On February 8, running back Kenneth Walker turned 29 offensive touches into 161 scrimmage yards as the Seattle Seahawks soundly defeated the New England Patriots in Super Bowl LX. Although Walker later held the Super Bowl MVP trophy on Levi’s Field in Santa Clara, California, that night was the final game of his four-year Seahawks […]
full_text: (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images On February 8, running back Kenneth Walker turned 29 offensive touches into 161 scrimmage yards as the Seattle Seahawks soundly defeated the New England Patriots in Super Bowl LX. Although Walker later held the Super Bowl MVP trophy on Levi’s Field in Santa Clara, California, that night was the final game of his four-year Seahawks career. Walker hit the open free agency market and quickly signed a three-year contract with the Kansas City Chiefs worth over $14 million annually. Early returns suggest the Chiefs got a bargain—and the Seahawks may have committed a major personnel blunder. Walker leads the league with 665 rushing yards. That total is particularly eye-opening because the Chiefs have already had their bye week, and Walker has one less game played than the next three running backs on the cumulative list. Conversely, the Seahawks only have 643 rushing yards as a team over six games. In Week 7, the Chiefs will travel to Seattle to face the Seahawks — and many of Walker’s former teammates — on “Sunday Night Football.” Expect the league’s top rusher to keep a low profile on the homecoming aspect. “It’s been smooth,” Walker said on Friday about his feelings on the matchup. “I’m treating it like any other week. I’m just getting the plan down and getting ready for Sunday night.” Earlier in the week, head coach Andy Reid expressed confidence that Walker would handle the Seattle return appropriately — particularly the extra burden of preparing against defenders who will be very familiar with his game. “He’s wired right to do it,” Reid remarked on Wednesday. “One thing when you’re on a team, everybody knows your strengths and weaknesses and your quirks and everything else. So, I’m sure the boys there will try to get after him a little bit, but he’s a pretty level-headed guy. The way he plays, you’re getting a good rep when he gets the ball in his hands. He’s kind of got one speed. He’s coming at you. It really doesn’t matter, I don’t think, who he’s playing, where he’s playing, all that.” At Lumen Field, one of the NFL’s loudest venues, the same fans who once cheered on Walker will now try to throw him off. He may also face on-field trash-talk from former teammates. “[Walker] knows it’s going to be loud,” Reid predicted, “and I’m sure his guys will be talking to him a little bit. He’s pretty level-headed that way. I think he has a pretty good idea of what to expect there, and that doesn’t mean they don’t like him and respect him, but that’s just what guys do. So, I’m sure they’ll try to give him the business. But he’s level-headed, and the kid’s got one speed. So, it doesn’t matter if he’s playing in a McDonald’s parking lot, he’s going to go fast — and that’s what he does and plays hard.” Walker has discussed his Seattle return with Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy, who played running back for three NFL teams. “It was mainly me and EB talking about how he went to a former team and how he felt about stuff and giving me pointers on stuff like that,” Walker recalled. “But you can’t make it bigger than what it is. I’m not the only one on this team; everybody’s going out there and playing a game. I don’t feel like it should be just about me, if that makes sense.” Walker’s most famous teammate agrees the Seahawks are one of a season’s worth of opponents, but expects the running back to have extra motivation. “I know it’s going to be a special moment for him,” said quarterback Patrick Mahomes on Wednesday. “You get to go back to the place where you kind of built your career, where you win a Super Bowl. I know how special that is being here. And those fans are kind of the people that were around him for all of that. And those are still a lot of the guys that were his teammates that he kind of grew up with as well in the NFL. “So, it’ll be a special moment for him. But at the end of the day, you’ve got to win a football game, and he knows that we have his back. We’re going to go out there and try to do whatever we can to win the game.”

title: Jim Harbaugh’s comments prove Chargers need new head coach
summary: Los Angeles Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh is in a really tough spot. After losing the team’s first six games, people are looking to him for answers as to why things have gone awry after making the playoffs in each of the last two years. Unfortunately for the Chargers, he is stumped. “We’re going to […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - OCTOBER 18: Head coach Jim Harbaugh of the Los Angeles Chargers watches pregame warmups prior to the game against the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images Los Angeles Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh is in a really tough spot. After losing the team’s first six games, people are looking to him for answers as to why things have gone awry after making the playoffs in each of the last two years. Unfortunately for the Chargers, he is stumped. “We’re going to look at everything,” Harbaugh said via the team’s website. “The job I’m doing, it starts with me. The plan is to watch this and get with our offensive coaches. “I see the effort, the work being put in, in the meetings and the practice field. To get that to translate to the field is what’s necessary,” Harbaugh added. “I feel bad for our players, our team, our coaches, our fans. It needs to be addressed.” Sometimes this is how things go in the NFL: a few plays go one way, a team doesn’t live up to its potential in one week, and a snowball effect forms. That appears to be what’s happened with the Chargers, who are one of two winless teams in the NFL going into Week 7. With Harbaugh not truly figuring out how to fix the issue, it’s clear that he needs to point the finger at himself. This doesn’t mean Harbaugh is a bad coach. It just means he doesn’t know how to coach this group beyond what he was able to do in these past two years. That’s why coaching changes happen, and it comes at an unfortunate time. Whether the Chargers fire Harbaugh in the middle of the season or wait until the end of the year, it’s clear that a new voice is needed to put this team in the right direction. Harbaugh has taken this team as far as it can go, and the closest way to moving higher up the ladder is to start from scratch. BFTB community, should the Chargers fire Harbaugh in the middle of the season? Let us know in the comments section below.

title: Rams were right to not wait for 2027 QB class
summary: The Los Angeles Rams drafted quarterback Ty Simpson with the 13th overall pick this year and that was probably higher than any other team would have taken the inexperienced Alabama signal-caller, but the reason Les Snead did it was: Opportunity. The Rams didn’t expect to have a high first-round pick in 2027 — they would […]
full_text: The Los Angeles Rams drafted quarterback Ty Simpson with the 13th overall pick this year and that was probably higher than any other team would have taken the inexperienced Alabama signal-caller, but the reason Les Snead did it was: Opportunity. The Rams didn’t expect to have a high first-round pick in 2027 — they would later trade it for Myles Garrett anyway — and Simpson was the best available of a weak bunch. Some argued that even the sixth or seventh-best quarterback in 2027 would be a better prospect than Simpson. A “historic” class, they said. Arch you sure about that? Because Manning, I’ve got some news for you … For most of 2023 to 2025, the media and many fans were practically desperate to proclaim that Arch Manning would become the next great NFL quarterback, anointing him as a future number one overall pick even before he enrolled at Texas as the top prospect in the country. Manning’s star was so bright that it also shone a light on many other quarterbacks expected to be available in the 2027 class, some of whom would be first-time eligible and others who returned to college for more NIL money. Dante Moore, C.J. Carr, Drew Mestemaker, LaNorris Sellers, Trinidad Chambliss, Darian Mensah, Julian Sayin, and Jayden Maiava to name eight. ESPN’s Jordan Reid recently posted a big board in which he had zero quarterbacks in the top-7, until Mestemaker lands at eight, and then there isn’t another QB until Chambliss at 15. There are just three QBs in the top-20 and Manning is now being projected to go back to school for a fifth season — perhaps not at Texas. NEW: Arch Manning took significantly fewer first-team reps with Texas’ first-team offense this week than he typically does, ESPN reports. Backup KJ Lacey Jr. had a precipitous uptick in first-team reps. https://t.co/jx1sPSqDOH pic.twitter.com/zF4APo9SYj — On3 (@On3) October 24, 2026 2027 Mock Drafts were eager to put five or six quarterbacks in the top-10 — to a sickening degree — and to argue that the entire landscape of the league could be altered by the “Manning Class”. At worst, the 2027 draft should resemble classes in 2018, 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024, when quarterbacks were heavily concentrated in the top-5 or top-12 picks. I mean, right there are five recent classes that had at least three quarterbacks get drafted immediately, and 2027 was being cited as better than ALL of them. But two months into the college season, the Manning Class looks more like a Clowning Class. By getting to spend 2026 with Ty Simpson, giving him an extra year of development and NFL coaching, did the Rams actually get a better quarterback prospect than anyone they could have had in 2027? What went wrong with Arch and company? If you are like me and you have always said that Arch Manning is the most overrated prospect of the century, please leave a comment below so I know I’m not alone on this hill. I know I wasn’t, but it was hard to get a word in like “But…. why? ” when you’ve got practically every draft analyst in the industry making excuses for Manning and telling us we didn’t “know ball” because not all of us were ready to call him a future first-round pick. He has never done anything on a football field that suggests he’s a first-round pick, let alone first overall. Yet you had everyone from Todd McShay to Mel Kiper to Field Yates arguing the opposite. Maybe they’d bring up ONE play or ONE trait, but at the end of the day if his name was “Arch Munning” we wouldn’t even know about him. (Except maybe to giggle that there’s a QB named “Munning”.) "I'll go with the Oregon quarterback over Arch [Manning]. I'll go Dante Moore." @MoveTheSticks believes that Oregon's Dante Moore can be the No. 1 overall pick in the 2027 NFL draft 👀 (via @RichEisenShow ) pic.twitter.com/iFujfzIdJB — NFL on ESPN (@ESPNNFL) April 27, 2026 This rant is not about Arch Manning, it’s about the media/draft ecosystem that allows analysts to spread misinformation about a prospect for clicks, views, or simply out of peer pressure. The Internet is not a welcoming place for dissenting views, let’s be honest. Here’s a very brief Manning timeline: He dominated high schoolers in 2A division class with no other real Division I prospects Even then, Manning’s team would lose badly in the playoffs every year (an elite QB should be enough under those circumstances) He sat as a true freshman—which is fine He sat as a sophomore too—which is not fine, especially when the starter is Quinn Ewers In his third year with Steve Sarkisian, he starts his career throwing five picks in five games Including picks against UTEP and San Jose State Manning got praised for finishing strong in 2025, but even at the end of the year he averaged under 7 yards per attempt and he was supposed to be surrounded by one of the best teams in the country. Although Arch Manning may have gotten drafted over Fernando Mendoza this year — maybe — did he go back to school for more seasoning or did he go back because he heard from the NFL that he wouldn’t go as high as everyone expected? Because to the Mannings, it would be embarrassing if Arch had all this hype and wasn’t drafted top-5, top-10, or even ahead of Ty Simpson. Ty Simpson was a better player than Arch Manning in 2025, after all. Better by a lot. Having now lost back-to-back games against unranked opponents, Texas is considering benching Manning for a true freshman. According to Tom Pelissero, he texted someone familiar with Manning and was told that it’s more likely that Manning is at Ole Miss next season than he is in the NFL Draft. “I texted one person who’s known Arch (Manning) a long time earlier tonight, and I said, ‘Where do you see Arch in 2027?’ And his response was Ole Miss.” — @TomPelissero on the latest Bill Simmons Podcast Manning and Texas will host Ole Miss this weekend. — Josh Ward (@Josh_Ward) October 23, 2026 To some people these developments are shocking. To some of us, it was apparent as soon as Manning spent a second year behind Ewers that something was wrong with this picture. Manning isn’t the only Faller Daniel Jeremiah and many others claimed that actually Dante Moore was the elite future MVP candidate in the 2027 QB Class. But Moore suffered a serious head injury against USC and will miss his third straight game. Oregon QB Dante Moore has been ruled OUT for Saturday’s game vs. Illinois. Moore will miss his third straight game as he continues to recover from a concussion. pic.twitter.com/yjsb68ANzz — Yahoo Sports (@YahooSports) October 22, 2026 Moore is now just 37th on Reid’s big board. Some see C.J. Carr as the best prospect in the draft. Despite an impressive TD/INT ratio of 16:1, Carr is seen as merely having average traits and being a borderline first-round pick , not a lock. Tested against the BYU defense last week, Carr was held to just 261 yards and no touchdowns on 49 passes as Notre Dame lost for the first time. It seems like every year someone is saying that LaNorris Sellers is about to prove he’s the next Lamar Jackson. But he’s a career 63% passer, throws too many picks, and hasn’t come anywhere close to Lamar’s rushing stats. Julian Sayin was supposed to be the next great Ohio State quarterback who would go into the draft as a top pick. But unimpressive physical traits never matched his Buckeyes-juiced stats and now he’s out indefinitely with an arm injury. Ohio State coach Ryan Day said that QB Julian Sayin is out indefinitely. There’s a plan being put in place for Sayin not being available for both the regular season and postseason. He said there’s no specific timeline on the recovery. He’s dealing with an injury on his throwing… pic.twitter.com/b3AZ669S21 — Pete Thamel (@PeteThamel) October 20, 2026 Instead, many mock drafters have turned to Oklahoma State’s Drew Mestemaker as the last hope of the 2027 draft. But not even Mestemaker is getting projected as the number one pick. That’s almost always Ohio State receiver Jeremiah Smith now. Reid cites Mestemaker’s quick ascension as an…

title: Cowherd: Rams fans don’t know full Puka Nacua story
summary: Puka Nacua has been the subject of many stories over the last three years, both really positive and really negative. We know the Los Angeles Rams have been aware of the negative stories that get reported, but how many haven’t reached the media or the public yet? At least a few, according to Colin Cowherd, […]
full_text: Puka Nacua has been the subject of many stories over the last three years, both really positive and really negative. We know the Los Angeles Rams have been aware of the negative stories that get reported , but how many haven’t reached the media or the public yet? At least a few, according to Colin Cowherd, and that why it’s been so difficult for the Rams to come to a decision on his future with the team. “(The Rams) have been putting out fires behind the scenes for three years (for Puka). You’ve read about some of them,” says Cowherd. How much worse could it get? "They've been putting out fires behind the scenes for three years. You've read about some of them." – Colin Cowherd on Puka Nacua pic.twitter.com/8bdHJXqpCR — Awful Announcing (@awfulannouncing) October 23, 2026 As the Rams go into Sunday’s game against the Raiders without Davante Adams, they are also unsure if Nacua will be able to go either after suffering a calf injury in practice . Nacua already missed two games earlier this season and he also missed six games in 2024. Nacua left several games in 2025 and miraculously only missed one game. If that’s all the information you had, it would be easy to let Puka walk over $40-$45 million in annual salary when he’s a free agent in 2027. Even without Cowherd’s alleged extra issues we don’t know about. But it’s not that easy. The Rams are so clearly a worse team without Puka Nacua and on the field they need him more than he needs them . If L.A. doesn’t want Puka, other teams will. He’ll get paid either way, he’ll get targeted 10-15 times per game when he’s healthy on any team. Matthew Stafford targeted Puka 24 times against the Bills. Les Snead is already looking at a roster that probably won’t — and definitely shouldn’t — bring back Davante Adams next year. They don’t know if Stafford will be back after this season. We don’t even know if Sean McVay will coach the team in 2027. Without Puka, the Rams would definitely be in the running for least-talented offense in the NFL. On the other hand, what if Nacua’s injuries are never going to stop? What if Cowherd’s trying to not-so-subtly tell us that Nacua is facing more serious allegations? We don’t know what the Rams are going to do We apparently don’t know what Puka Nacua already did.
