summary: Help is on the way for the Seattle Seahawks’ offensive line. After right guard Anthony Bradford was designated to return on Monday, the Seahawks activated him off injured reserve ahead of the team’s Week 7 prime-time clash against the Kansas City Chiefs. Wide receiver Montorie Foster Jr, one of the stars and feel-good stories from […]
full_text: Help is on the way for the Seattle Seahawks’ offensive line. After right guard Anthony Bradford was designated to return on Monday, the Seahawks activated him off injured reserve ahead of the team’s Week 7 prime-time clash against the Kansas City Chiefs. Wide receiver Montorie Foster Jr, one of the stars and feel-good stories from HBO’s ‘Hard Knocks’ series, was waived in a corresponding move. Foster had been a healthy scratch since Week 2 and his only snaps in Week 1 were on special teams. The fourth-year guard has been out since shortly after Seattle’s Week 1 win over the New England Patriots, missing practice ahead of the Week 2 win over the Cardinals with knee and hip injuries. Ultimately, he was downgraded to out and then placed on injured reserve — but with head coach Mike Macdonald stating at the time his I.R. stint would be on the “shorter side.” Similarly, Bradford’s return to practice this week included further optimism from Macdonald, who said, “Normally I’m pretty coy on this one, but it’s pretty straightforward. If he has a good week, he’s gonna play a significant amount or the whole game.” Sure enough, Bradford will now be back in the lineup against the undefeated Chiefs after practicing all week and having no injury designation. Regardless of Sunday’s opponent, his return will give a much-needed boost to an offensive line that has struggled to protect Sam Darnold in 2026. Through six games, Seattle has allowed 16 sacks while Darnold has faced a league-high pressure rate of 34.5%. Bradford, a fourth-round pick of the Seahawks in the 2023 NFL Draft, started all 17 games last season after making 21 starts across his first two years in Seattle.

title: 5Qs, 5As: Kenneth Walker returns to Lumen primetime Seahawks-Chiefs matchup
summary: It’s Week 7, and the championship defense of the Seattle Seahawks is not going as many fans had hoped. A turnover plagued offense has allowed opponents to put easy points on the board, and the result is a 3-3 record that would have Mike Macdonald and his team watching the playoffs from home if the […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - DECEMBER 24: George Karlaftis #56 of the Kansas City Chiefs tackles Kenneth Walker III #9 of the Seattle Seahawks during the second quarter at Arrowhead Stadium on December 24, 2022 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s Week 7, and the championship defense of the Seattle Seahawks is not going as many fans had hoped. A turnover plagued offense has allowed opponents to put easy points on the board, and the result is a 3-3 record that would have Mike Macdonald and his team watching the playoffs from home if the season ended today. Luckily, however, there is plenty of season left to right the ship, with the first opportunity to do so Sunday against the undefeated Kansas City Chiefs. Joining Field Gulls to preview the primetime showdown is Maurice Elston of Arrowhead Pride, and here are the answers provided to the questions posed this week. 1. Kenneth Walker has been phenomenal so far this season. How has Andy Reid taken advantage of Walker’s skills to rely less on Patrick Mahomes as Mahomes works his way back from the knee injury he suffered late last season? It may feel like Andy Reid has completely transformed the Chiefs into a run-first offense, but the numbers say the change has been more subtle. Kansas City ran the ball on 40.5% of its offensive plays last season, compared with approximately 43.5% this year. The Chiefs have increased their rushing attempts from 25.3 to roughly 29 per game, but that is not an overwhelming difference. The results are where you see Kenneth Walker III’s impact. Kansas City averaged 4.2 yards per rushing attempt last season, but even that number was boosted significantly by Patrick Mahomes. Mahomes gained 422 yards on 64 carries, averaging 6.6 yards per attempt. The Chiefs’ running backs combined for only 1,247 yards on 336 carries—approximately 3.7 yards per attempt. Without Mahomes’ rushing production, Kansas City averaged only 3.8 yards per carry as a team. Walker is now averaging 6.3 yards per attempt with 665 rushing yards through five games. So while Reid is calling slightly more running plays, the dramatic difference is that the Chiefs now have a running back producing at an elite level. Mahomes no longer has to scramble to provide the offense’s most efficient rushing plays. The biggest schematic adjustment Reid has made is putting Mahomes under center more frequently. Before Walker arrived, many of Kansas City’s runs came from shotgun or pistol formations. Reid saw how successful Walker was taking handoffs from under center in Seattle and incorporated more of those concepts into the Chiefs’ offense. That change has created a legitimate play-action passing game. Defenses must respect Walker, which slows down the pass rush and gives Mahomes more time to operate. Reid can also move Mahomes outside the pocket off play action, simplifying his reads and protecting his knee. More than simply calling additional runs, the improved efficiency, timing of those calls and formations Kansas City is using have relieved pressure on Mahomes. 2. Kansas City has steamrolled its opponents so far this season, but it has had the benefit of playing a relatively weak schedule thus far. The Chiefs are obviously a high-level team, but is there any concern that a change in strength of schedule could lead to more than just speed bumps in the coming weeks and months? I don’t believe Kansas City’s schedule looked nearly as weak before the season as people are making it sound now. Yes, the upcoming schedule is considerably more difficult, but many people probably would have predicted the Chiefs to be 2-3 or 3-2 through their first five games. Denver won the AFC West last season and reached the AFC Championship Game. The Chargers swept Kansas City last year and entered this season as one of the popular picks to win the division. Nobody expected Los Angeles to begin this season 0-6. The Raiders were undefeated when the Chiefs traveled to Las Vegas, and they pushed Kansas City to the final possession. Indianapolis took the Chiefs to overtime. Miami was probably the only opponent most people viewed as a game Kansas City should clearly win. It is fair to point out that some of those teams have struggled since playing the Chiefs, but Kansas City still had to beat them. Now the schedule becomes much harder, beginning with the defending Super Bowl champions in Seattle. Six of the Chiefs’ next eight games are on the road, and seven of their remaining opponents made the playoffs last season. That stretch will present challenges, but Kansas City is accustomed to playing a first-place schedule. This team has spent most of the Mahomes era receiving every opponent’s best effort. There will be speed bumps, but I’m not overly concerned about the schedule becoming something the Chiefs cannot handle. 3. Seahawks fans are familiar with the big names on the Chiefs’ roster. Who is someone whose name Seattle fans may not recognize on each side of the ball who could have an impact on the outcome Sunday night? On offense, I would go with left guard Kingsley Suamataia. That may sound strange because people normally expect a skill-position player when discussing someone under the radar, but Suamataia has quietly been one of Kansas City’s most consistent offensive players this season. When people discuss the Chiefs’ offensive line, Trey Smith and Creed Humphrey are usually the first names mentioned. Kahlil Benson receives attention because he is an undrafted rookie filling in for a former first-round pick at left tackle. Right tackle is always closely examined because of the questions Kansas City has had at that position. Suamataia, however, has become a dominant force at left guard. Before Kansas City’s fourth game, he had allowed pressure on only 3.8% of his pass-blocking opportunities, the lowest rate among starting left guards. Against the Chargers, he didn’t surrender a pressure over 31 pass-blocking snaps and earned a 90.3 run-blocking grade. The Chiefs consistently run behind him, and Walker has regularly found success on that side. On defense, I would watch rookie edge rusher R Mason Thomas. His traditional statistics may not jump off the page yet, but his natural pass-rushing ability is obvious. He generated five pressures against the Chargers, and his role continues to grow within Steve Spagnuolo’s defense. Sam Darnold is not the most mobile quarterback Kansas City will face, so Thomas’ speed off the edge could become a major factor if the Chiefs force Seattle into obvious passing situations. 4. Walker’s performance this season has come despite several injuries to expected starters on the Kansas City offensive line, and yet from the outside, it appears neither Walker nor the offense has missed a beat. Who should Seattle fans expect to see on the line for the Chiefs, and how well will the group perform against a defensive front that may be the toughest they have faced to this point in 2026? Seattle fans should expect Kahlil Benson at left tackle, Kingsley Suamataia at left guard, Creed Humphrey at center and Trey Smith at right guard. Right tackle remains the biggest question. Jaylon Moore left last week’s game with a concussion and has not practiced this week. If he does not clear the concussion protocol, Joshua Ezeudu could start after replacing him and playing 30 snaps against the Chargers. Ezeudu allowed one pressure but otherwise performed well in his first offensive action for Kansas City. Josh Simmons has officially been placed on injured reserve after his rehabilitation from a back injury plateaued, so the Chiefs will have Benson protecting Mahomes’ blind side for at least four more games. Benson has started all five games, but he remains an undrafted rookie preparing to face arguably the best defensive front Kansas City has seen this season. That must be a concern for the Chiefs. If Seattle creates an early lead and forces Kansas City into predictable passing situations, its…

full_text: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Each week we ask questions of the most plugged-in Seattle Seahawks fans and fans across the country. The Seattle Seahawks have been (relatively) down bad recently. They already have three losses, equaling the total from 2026. The road doesn’t get any easier with the Kansas City Chiefs and former Seahawks legend Kenneth Walker III returning to Lumen Field for a prime time matchup. Will Seattle be able to keep Walker under 100 yards, continuing their own defensive streak of holding rushers under that mark? That was the focus of this week’s poll . It wasn’t a total wipeout, but 61% of Seahawks fans think that Seattle will be able to contain last year’s Super Bowl MVP. Walker has been the workhorse for the Chiefs, leading the NFL in rushing. Seattle, meanwhile, has seen their running game stuck in neutral for the most part with Jadarian Price on IR and Zach Charbonnet still recovering from last year’s knee injury. Seattle hasn’t allowed a 100-yard rusher in nearly two calendar years – a streak which spans 35 games including playoffs. Something has to give on Sunday Night Football . Meanwhile on the fan confidence front, less than half of respondents believe the team is headed in the right direction. That’s a pretty damning statistic for the defending Super Bowl champions. However, I get it. The Seahawks haven’t played close to their potential, giving the ball away like it’s going out of style. Their defense has held up its end of the bargain, but the offense has been inconsistent to say the least. The upcoming matchup with the undefeated Chiefs could be the turning point for the 2026 season. Win this one to get back on track, and the Seahawks could be set up for a big run. And if they lose a third game in a row? Let’s just say the generally gloomy Seattle autumn will seem like rainbows and sunshine in comparison. title: Could the Seahawks actually trade away a running back?
summary: With the NFL trade deadline looming, there is lots of discussion about who the Seattle Seahawks could trade for. However, the trade deadline works both ways, and the Seahawks could potentially be in position to trade away some of their own players. That is not to say that Seattle will be sellers this trade season […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - JANUARY 17: Zach Charbonnet #26 of the Seattle Seahawks enters the field during player introductions prior to an NFL divisional playoff football game against the San Francisco 49ers at Lumen Field on January 17, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images With the NFL trade deadline looming, there is lots of discussion about who the Seattle Seahawks could trade for . However, the trade deadline works both ways, and the Seahawks could potentially be in position to trade away some of their own players. That is not to say that Seattle will be sellers this trade season – they are still Super Bowl contenders despite their 3-3 record. However, if Seattle were to make a trade for another running back, along with Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price nearing a return from injury, suddenly Seattle’s running back room could get too crowded. With that, let’s look at why Seattle could potentially be interested in trading one of their running backs away. The argument for making a run at a running back like Saquon Barkley, Jonathan Taylor, or Tony Pollard is that they can automatically bring a spark to the running back room that has struggled mightily this season. Yes, Zach Charbonnet is about to return from his ACL injury and Jadarian Price is only a few weeks away. However, Price has yet to show that he is ready to shoulder the load of an NFL offense, and Charbonnet, is on an expiring contract. Plus with Charbonnet, you never know how a player will look post ACL-surgery. Hopefully he is back to normal, however, Seattle needs to be prepared in case he doesn’t look like the Charbonnet of old. However, Seattle may need to put some of their own running backs on the trade block to help facilitate a trade for a Barkley, Taylor, or Pollard. That would include Emanuel Wilson, George Holani, or even Charbonnet, all three of which are on expiring contracts. If Seattle were to make a move for another running back, that would be a clear signal that none of these three running backs are in the Seahawks plans post-2026. Zach Charbonnet Charbonnet is coming back from his ACL-injury. Typically, other teams will not be interested in making a move for a player who has not proven that he is back to his old self. However, with the trade deadline being November 10th, the Seahawks could audition Charbonnet for a few weeks, show that he is back to his old self and use him as a chip to add to a package for another running back. All of that being said, in my opinion, Charbonnet would be the least likely of the Seahawks’ running backs to be shipped off. Charbonnet is a huge locker room presence, and to trade him away after a long, grueling, and miraculously quick ACL rehab process would likely shake the locker room in a negative way. George Holani or Emanuel Wilson On the other hand, Wilson and Holani are also both on expiring contracts. If Seattle were to trade for a running back, neither of these players would likely see the field on offense again, which would make them even more expendable. Holani has struggled mightily this season (although he did show some juice against the Denver Broncos in week six). Holani’s history of being a solid pass blocker and pass catcher could give him some interest as part of a trade package. Wilson, despite his clear athletic limitations, has been a slight sign of light in the otherwise dark and fainthearted Seahawks run game. It is this sign of light that could allow Wilson to have interest in a trade package as well. Despite signing with the Seahawks this past offseason, the Wilson signing always felt like a bandaid until Charbonnet returned from injury. Now that Charbonnet is back, Wilson is a logical trade package candidate – or even straight trade candidate, regardless if Seattle is using him to obtain another running back. Robert Henry Jr. or Velus Jones Jr. At the bottom of the depth chart are Henry Jr. and Jones Jr. The Seahawks just signed Henry Jr. off of the Washington Commanders practice squad. Considering this recent move, along with having Henry Jr. under contract for three seasons would all point to him not being a player John Schneider would want to move off of. Plus, Henry Jr. went undrafted in 2026 and was free to join any other 53-man roster for most of the 2026 season. This all indicates that other teams would not likely be interested in Henry Jr. as part of a trade package. Meanwhile, Jones Jr. has been on and off of the Seahawks active roster and practice squad. This also indicates that Jones Jr. would not move the needle much in any trade package the Seahawks could offer. Prediction Just to make a fool out of myself, here is a trade proposal that could make sense for another running back. Jonathan Taylor to Seattle for Emanuel Wilson, 2nd round pick, 3rd round pick . With Seattle having a plethora of 2027 draft picks (including multiple 3rd round picks) , giving up 2nd and 3rd round picks would be easy to make this trade happen. The bigger question is if the Colts would accept such a package. If Taylor is indeed on the move, the Seahawks will likely be in a bidding war. Two day-two draft picks, plus a serviceable running back in Wilson may be enough to make this happen. In this hypothetical trade, this would leave Seattle with the following depth chart. Velus Jones Jr. (contract through 2026) Jonathan Taylor (contract through 2027) Jadarian Price (contract through 2029/30 with 5th year option) Zach Charbonnet (contract through 2026) George Holani (contract through 2026) Robert Henry Jr. (contract through 2028) What do you think of this hypothetical trade? title: Why the Seahawks may not trade for Jonathan Taylor
summary: It’s no secret that the Seattle Seahawks want to be a running team but have been unable to jumpstart their offense with the ground game. Could a team that just fired its general manager, and may be holding a fire sale, be the answer to helping the Hawks solve this issue? Principal owner of the […]
full_text: It’s no secret that the Seattle Seahawks want to be a running team but have been unable to jumpstart their offense with the ground game. Could a team that just fired its general manager, and may be holding a fire sale, be the answer to helping the Hawks solve this issue? Principal owner of the Indianapolis Colts, Carlie Irsay-Gordon made the decision to relieve Chris Ballard of his post as GM this past week. This comes after Indy looked like a surprising contender early last season with Daniel Jones at the helm, then went all-in with blockbuster trade for CB, Sauce Gardner. Unfortunately for them, Jones was lost for the season shortly after. This year’s Colts team hasn’t looked the same and has sputtered to a 2-4 start. Pushing the chips to the middle ended in disaster, and it could ultimately cause the team in Indiana to clean house and sell off assets in order to enter a rebuild. One of the most prominent players involved in trade speculation is a running back who is tied for 7th league-wide in rushing yardage per game (82) and is in a 6-way tie for tops in rushing touchdowns (7) among RB’s: Jonathan Taylor. View Link Taylor is a great back. Thoughts of J.T. rampaging through defenses to keep Sam Darnold ahead of the sticks and in advantageous situations is undoubtedly a really fun idea that would give fans immediate confidence. But do they need to? I don’t think it’ll happen, for a few reasons. I get it. Taylor is a ready-made superstar at the position. One who is fast, powerful and durable. BUT when I see 12’s suggesting we send Jadarian Price and future picks for a soon-to-be 28-year-old… I just don’t think that’s how Schneider operates. Especially not at the halfback position. This team has championship repeat aspirations, but Seattle is not going to sell the farm to make it happen. Price has a future here as a playmaker. Caveat : I don’t have any personal connection to or 100% accurate bead on GM, John Schneider. He is unafraid of taking big swings when he deems it warranted. Schneider has repeatedly mentioned how he likes to save some gun powder to make improvements in-season. He has shocked us before… but we can surmise some things when looking at the way he operates. Schneider stated back in March that the running back is “a position that… you can find guys.” They could’ve paid Ken Walker. Actually, bump that: they could’ve at least made an offer to K9 . A working theory is that the writing was really already on the wall for both sides, any way you want to slice it. Walker was unhappy in not having his talents maximized and may currently feel slightly justified about that, as he tears up the league for the Kansas City Chiefs. From the Seahawks’ perspective, Walker priced himself into holding the leverage for a possible once-in-a-lifetime type of running back contract after a magical postseason run on the way to a Super Bowl trophy and Super Bowl MVP award. There’s also the fact that Taylor signed a 3-year contract this past offseason and averages a cap hit of ~$20M over the life of that deal. If the team were to cut him next year, they could but would incur a $10M dead cap hit. That’s more than Walker III is getting paid! Ever since Marshawn Lynch left, the Seahawks shifted to more of a running-back-by-committee approach, rather than the bell cow model. In the four seasons where Marshawn Lynch played in more than 12 games for the Seattle Seahawks, he averaged over 295 carries per year. Chris Carson has been the only one since to clock more than 230 carries in a season, with 247 and 278 in back-to-back years (both over 1.1K rushing yards). Ken Walker was the next closest thing, taking 228 attempts in his rookie season and 221 in his final year in Seattle. Other than those standout seasons, the Seahawks have platooned players like Christine Michael, C.J. Prosise, Thomas Rawls, Rashaad Penny, Zach Charbonnet, Carson, Walker and others. The Seattle Seahawks under Mike Macdonald have committed to a Shanahan-style run game. That is an offensive system that attacks with outside zone run concepts, play-action and (more recently) quarterback pocket movement. It’s not named after Kyle, although the younger Shanahan deserves credit for innovating the system forward. His father, Mike Shanahan, was a pioneer in this aspect, and weaponized a wide array of seemingly anonymous backs to great effect. Terrell Davis was a sixth-round pick and is now a Hall-of-Famer. Olandis Gary was a fourth-Rounder who popped out to be a 1,100-yard rusher. Mike Anderson was taken in the sixth, yet went on to win OROY with over 1,400 on the ground and 15 TD’s. Reuben Droughns was a converted fullback! Denver went with him, feeling good enough about it to trade the great Clinton Portis for Champ Bailey. Remember Tatum Bell? The Shanahan offensive scheme de-prioritizes running back financial commitments in favor of emphasizing the line and other aspects of the offense/defense. This could explain the mentality in letting Kenneth Walker leave without even an offer. The Seattle Seahawks are leaning into what they believe is an advantage of this offensive structure and team approach to the running game. Having that been said, the Seahawks do have multiple players returning soon, and one is a recent 1st-round pick. Seahawks team reporter, John Boyle iterated reasoning for no panic very succinctly: “how it will shake out with Zach Charbonnet expected back soon, possibly this week, and with first-round pick Jadarian Price not far behind. The Seahawks will always look at every option, but that position won’t seem like as much of a need in the next couple of weeks as it might at this very moment.” Wilson seems to be a fine third back; a back who can be a bruiser, a closer and a change-of-pace runner. He has, at least, given this team a chance during his run as starter. Working behind Charbonnet and Price (who could be the future tandem, if Charbs comes back on a favorable deal) might form a much stronger rushing attack than when Seattle was feeding former Bears WR, Velus Jones Jr. rushing attempts. Funny thing is that Seahawks backs are forcing missed tackles at a strong rate… but gaining yards before being contacted at a lower rate than the rest of the league. RB Yards Before Contact & Missed Tackles Forced pic.twitter.com/DQVHChRyKb — Jrfortgang (@throwthedamball) October 21, 2026 That makes one think… maybe a different position should be on the docket. 🤔

title: 49ers vs. Falcons: How to watch, game time, and betting odds
summary: The San Francisco 49ers’ injuries keep coming, and they keep winning anyway. Now they go into Week 7 with their most injury-depleted wide receiver room yet and travel to face the Atlanta Falcons. Should the 49ers manage to win, they will head into their bye week at 7-0 and maintain their modest 3-game (at least—depending […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 19: Jordan Elliott #92 of the San Francisco 49ers celebrates making a stop with teammates during the second half of an NFL football game against the Atlanta Falcons at Levi's Stadium on October 19, 2025 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers’ injuries keep coming, and they keep winning anyway. Now they go into Week 7 with their most injury-depleted wide receiver room yet and travel to face the Atlanta Falcons. Should the 49ers manage to win, they will head into their bye week at 7-0 and maintain their modest 3-game (at least—depending on what happens Sunday night) lead in the NFC West. At the same time, even the 49ers have to give up a game at some point, and the Falcons may have the makings of a trap game. This will be a morning game on FOX with the dreaded 10:00 AM start time. Kenny Albert will handle play-by-play, while Greg Olsen will provide color. The 49ers are playing on a shortened week after beating the Washington Commanders 23-17 on Monday Night Football. The recap is simple: The 49ers offense showed up in the first half, and then the defense saved everyone’s bacon in the closing seconds. The Commanders could have stolen that game had the defense not stepped it up in the final seconds, or Malik Mustapha wasn’t flying around the field laying the wood. Where did things go sideways? It can be pinpointed to when wide receiver Mike Evans went into the locker room. Once that happened, the 49ers offense took a step backwards. At the end of the day, the 49ers defensive line, without Nick Bosa, stepped up and made some plays to save the game and put the 49ers up 6-0. They won, but these injuries make them increasingly vulnerable. The Falcons appeared to be looking like a sleeper team after their Week 3, 35-14 victory over the Green Bay Packers. They followed it up in Week 4 with a 45-24 thumping of the New Orleans Saints. Some were saying this was a possible playoff team thanks in part to their running game led by running back Bijan Robinson. During this two-game stretch, it was argued he may be the best running back in the league. Unfortunately, both the Packers and Saints had losing records entering those games. After those victories came losses to the Baltimore Ravens and Chicago Bears—two teams that entered their games against the Falcons with a winning record and two teams Robinson failed to amass at least 100 yards rushing against. The Bears in particular held the Falcons to seven points until the fourth quarter. The offense goes through Robinson and if the 49ers can find a way to slow him down, that seems to be the key to defeating the Falcons. Could this be a trap game? The 49ers are favored by only 2.5 points on the road and have injuries that somewhat level the playing field. Evans’ injury in the aforementioned Monday Night game was revealed to be Achilles soreness, which will keep him out for this game. Like Robinson, the offense runs through Evans, so this is a major blow. They did get some help with activating wide receiver Christian Kirk; he’ll make his season debut against Atlanta . Evans, as we’ve said, is out. This is along with Nick Bosa (calf), Deebo Samuel (hamstring), safety Marques Sigel (ankle), linebacker Luke Gifford (groin), and linebacker Garret Wallow (hamstring). Special teamer Siran Neal and cornerback Upton Stout are questionable. Should the 49ers get through this week, they can enter the BYE and get some much-needed rest for the second half-ish of their schedule. In a strange twist, the Falcons injury report is longer than the 49ers though the names of players out for Sunday are not on the level of people like Evans and Bosa. Out for the Falcons is running back Brian Robinson Jr., linebacker Divine Deablo, defensive back Billy Bowman Jr., and offensive tackle Michael Jerrell. title: Fred Warner gets fined over $65,000 for two uncalled penalties
summary: San Francisco 49ers players have been issued some major fines over the past two weeks for hits that went uncalled during games. Two weeks ago, Malik Mustapha was fined nearly $7,000 for an unnecessary roughness hit on the 49ers’ final defensive drive in their 32-29 win over the Seattle Seahawks. The hit came on an […]
full_text: (Photo by Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) | Getty Images San Francisco 49ers players have been issued some major fines over the past two weeks for hits that went uncalled during games. Two weeks ago, Malik Mustapha was fined nearly $7,000 for an unnecessary roughness hit on the 49ers’ final defensive drive in their 32-29 win over the Seattle Seahawks. The hit came on an incompletion to Jaxon Smith-Njigba and went uncalled. At the time, the Seahawks were at midfield, trailing by three with a 1st & 10. The play was incomplete, and the Seahawks couldn’t get any yards on their next three plays, resulting in a turnover on downs and a loss. Had they gotten the penalty, perhaps we would have seen a different outcome at the end of that game. Then, this past week, Fred Warner was fined $65,673 for two separate unnecessary roughness plays: $17,911 for a hit on a defenseless player and $47,762 for use of the helmet. The first play saw a flag thrown and then picked up, with the broadcast saying in real time that it should’ve been a penalty. The second play, a hit on tight end Chig Okonkwo, went uncalled. The Okonkwo play came with 7:12 left in the fourth quarter on 2nd & 8 on a short pass to the flat off play-action. The Commanders did end up picking up the first down on that drive and went all the way down the field on a 13-play, 61-yard drive that resulted in a turnover on downs. This is the fourth time Warner has been fined this season, with the fines totaling over $100,000. Back in Week 3, he was fined $41.793 for two violations against Arizona Cardinals tight end Trey McBride, with one penalty being illegal use of the helmet and the other being a hip-drop tackle that went uncalled. If Warner gets called twice more for hits on defenseless players, he could face a one-game suspension. Warner also has two penalties for use of the helmet this season.

The team removed Christian Kirk’s questionable status for Sunday’s game against the Atlanta Falcons and officially activated him from the Injured Reserve List. With Mike Evans ruled out, Here’s a look at the wide receiver depth chart heading into Week 7: Brandin Cooks Jordan Watkins Jacob Cowing Kirk It’ll be interesting to see if this is one of those games where Brock Purdy sprays the ball around to every pass catcher on the field, or if Christian McCaffrey sees another spike in his usage since the 49ers have a week off coming up for him to rest. None of these players play special teams, other than Cowing serving as the returner. That means the 49ers will only have four wideouts active against Atlanta, who also just made their best cornerback, A.J. Terrell, available. It’s also a game where we could see Kyle Shanahan lean on George Kittle. The Falcons allow the third-most targets and fourth-most receiving yards to tight ends. They limit the big play, but concede underneath. That could work in the 49ers’ favor. The team brought edge rusher Ogbo Okoronkwo back to the practice squad and released defensive tackle Kevin Givens. So, linebacker Jalen Graham and Okoronkwo were elevated from the practice squad to the active roster. Mykel Williams, Keion White, Okoronkwo, Romello Height, and Khalid Kareem will keep things steady until Nick Bosa returns. The unit has exceeded expectations. You could say the same for each individual, too.

title: Don’t expect an active trade deadline from the Bucs
summary: When a team starts 1-5, which more often than not means its season is already over, it’s common and reasonable to speculate on what changes will happen to set up for better success the next year. The Buccaneers are, for the first time in a long time, being speculated as sellers at the upcoming Nov. […]
full_text: TAMPA, FL - June 02: Tampa Bay Buccaneers General Manager Jason Licht and Head Coach Todd Bowles watch the team warm up during the Tampa Bay Buccaneers OTA workout on June 02, 2026 at the AdventHealth Training Center in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Cliff Welch/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images When a team starts 1-5, which more often than not means its season is already over, it’s common and reasonable to speculate on what changes will happen to set up for better success the next year. The Buccaneers are, for the first time in a long time, being speculated as sellers at the upcoming Nov. 10 trade deadline because of their situation. Historically, that is not something Tampa has entertained, and while it could change before then, fans shouldn’t expect them to deviate from that approach for a few reasons. Playoffs!? You’re Talking About Playoffs?? Statistically, there is a 1.1% chance of the Buccaneers making the playoffs. Only four teams have done it in modern history, with the 2020 Washington Football Team being the latest to accomplish the feat at 7-9 (you might remember them and who they happened to play). So yeah, chances are currently quite dire, but the Bucs get a tiny bump from the fact they still play in the NFC South. The division is often the butt of many jokes, and this season hasn’t done much to dissuade them — only the Panthers have a winning record at 3-2, and two of their wins come courtesy of a devastated Eagles team and a not-so-good Falcons team. That said, the next two games against Carolina and Atlanta are basically must-win to stay alive. If they do that, their chances at 3-5 with two division wins bump them up to 19% per the New York Times playoff simulator. It’s slight, but it’s a chance. The Buccaneers’ strength of schedule gets significantly easier in the second half of the year as well, currently ranking at 31st overall. For a team that hasn’t lost a game by more than one score all year, that is something to consider. For an embattled head coach hanging on by a thread, all those factors combined would keep eyes fully focused on the rest of this campaign. Remaining Strength of Schedule 1. MIN — hardest — 2. ATL 3. MIA … 30. DAL 31. TB 32. JAX — easiest —- pic.twitter.com/3ZNbIcafwe — SFdata9ers🏈📊 (@sfdata9ers) October 22, 2026 Many Bucs’ Contracts Are Not Trade-Friendly Plenty of fans have speculated that the Bucs could sell their high-priced, recognized franchise faces like Vita Vea (who was just extended) and Chris Godwin to net some significant draft capital. There is a big problem with that — it makes little financial sense to do so. Trading Godwin would save $15 million this season but accelerate $16 million in dead cap onto next year’s books. And currently, it’s hard to know just how valuable he still is. He’s having a career-worst start to a season, failing to net 50 yards or more in any contest so far. He still looks capable based on the eye test, but terrible quarterback play and a flawed scheme have deeply hindered him and the other Bucs’ receivers. His lack of production might make other teams hesitant to part with much, and at that point is it worth trading a franchise cornerstone and team leader for a late Day 3 pick? Chris Godwin on his limited role in Bucs’ 1-5 start: “It’s definitely been interesting, different than anything I’ve been through in my career … I’m trying to stick to the process and make sure I’m where I need to be.” — Greg Auman (@gregauman) October 21, 2026 For Vea, he is not playing well (just a 55.8 Pro Football Focus grade with only 9 pressures and no sacks) and he just got paid out a $21 million bonus, which is killer in terms of both real cash flow and cap implications. Unless some team really wants to pay a premium, like a third-round pick, for what he has done and not what he’s currently doing, it doesn’t feel like he’s going anywhere. Antoine Winfield Jr. has also been floated around, which makes the least sense because he also has a massive dead cap hit ($20 million) and he’s actually still good. The splash plays haven’t been as frequent, but he’s also not been put in positions to really do that — Todd Bowles has him operating as the ultimate leak stopper, which is an important but unglamorous job. More likely trade candidates, if any, would be names like running back Kenny Gainwell, defensive tackle A’Shawn Robinson, and edge rusher Yaya Diaby. Gainwell and Robinson are on cheap deals with a good history of production, and Diaby is on an expiring rookie contract in a season where he’s taken a step back rushing the passer. Diaby has 18 sacks in three seasons and is a steady presence in run defense — absolutely a useful player — but will he be worth a larger contract when the Bucs might be rebuilding / retooling and they’re currently getting a huge breakout from David Walker? The Bucs Are Loyal and Stubborn…To A Fault Most people know this already but the Bucs really trust their guys across the spectrum. From the roster all the way up the front office, Tampa places faith in its people and gives them room to operate. Despite general manager Jason Licht engineering a largely failing strategy between 2014 and 2019, the Glazers stuck with him and got rewarded in a massive way — Bruce Arians at head coach, Tom Brady at quarterback, one of the best rosters in the league, and a Super Bowl trophy. He’s earned a strong reputation as one of the strongest talent evaluators and drafters in the league since then, as the Bucs consistently rank as one of the best franchises in terms of rostering and keeping homegrown talent. While that’s generally a good trait to have, like anything it can be a double-edged sword, which the Bucs are being fully sliced by right now. Prominently, Todd Bowles should’ve been fired after last season. He’s underperformed at his job relative to the roster’s talent level for multiple years, most prominently last season when the Bucs started 6-2 and then collapsed to the tune of an 8-9 season and its first playoff-less season since 2019. Bowles has overseen a stretch of 1-5 or worse in all five seasons as head coach. He’s been slow to adapt to trends, is too hesitant to make bold decisions in regards to roster management and in-game decisions, and is way too loyal to some of his “guys.” And as good as Licht has been, he has enabled Bowles and the coaching staff. Why is Alex Anzalone still playing when he’s one of the worst linebackers in football? Why isn’t David Walker playing more despite he’s producing at an elite clip on limited snaps? These are just a couple questions THIS YEAR, as you could easily go back to several very questionable decisions throughout the years. Bucs' David Walker has four sacks this season despite playing only 99 defensive snaps in six games. There are 17 NFL players with 4+ sacks this season — the average defensive snaps in that group is 263. Walker is the lowest; only one close is Browns' Mason Graham (138). — Greg Auman (@gregauman) October 19, 2026 No general manager wants to undermine his head coach, and Licht is one of the best at not doing that. In fact, he’s done everything he can to supply Bowles with players who optimally fit his scheme, but sometimes you need to have the gumption to put your foot down and make roster decisions for the benefit of the whole team. Licht has not done that in recent times. They might’ve also made some massive missteps when it comes to committing to their “guys.” Baker Mayfield has largely been a net positive for this team, but since midway through 2025, he’s been a huge negative on the field. In what would’ve been a contract year for him, Mayfield spent the off-season talking a big game about his slighted feelings and carrying a Cleveland-sized chip on his shoulder. Well he got his big-money extension right before the dawn of the season despite not earning it on his most recent performances, and that’s looking like a critical error unless he hugely turns it around. We already…

title: Tyler’s Take – Adam Peters has the chance to play hero, but will he?
summary: Washington currently sits at 1-4-1 and in the basement of the weak NFC East. Despite this, they are just two games out of first with a very manageable eight games coming up. General manager Adam Peters is currently under a lot of heat for how he has handled roster building over the past two seasons […]
full_text: Washington currently sits at 1-4-1 and in the basement of the weak NFC East. Despite this, they are just two games out of first with a very manageable eight games coming up. General manager Adam Peters is currently under a lot of heat for how he has handled roster building over the past two seasons and his much-maligned choice at head coach in Dan Quinn, who currently sits on the hottest seat in the NFL coaching ranks. A lot of the criticism surrounding Peters has come from not adequately surrounding Jayden Daniels with the necessary pieces to succeed while he’s still on his rookie contract. This summer, he and Quinn lied for weeks to fans about the state of Washington’s center position, only to watch his prognostication go up in flames as the team benched his “wonder boy” center Nick Allegretti for poor play. Sticking with Chris Paul at left guard has proven to be a poor decision and the lack of depth at offensive tackle that forced Brandon Coleman to man the blindside has been a complete DISASTER! As we approach the 2026 NFL Trade deadline on November 10th at 4 p.m. ET, Peters has a chance to play hero for this struggling team. Will he rise to the occasion, or will he be content to smolder in the ashes of the fire he set? Trading for Quenton Nelson Quenton Nelson is rumored to be on the trade block as the deadline approaches. The Colts, who are 2-4, are said to be in full-blown sell mode and have a few stars, including Nelson, who are said to be available for the right compensation. Nelson is a 30-year-old, six-time All-Pro and eight-time Pro Bowler who is regarded as one of the best guards in the NFL. He was the sixth overall pick in the 2018 NFL Draft and has missed just four games in his eight-year career. In 2022, Nelson signed a four-year, $80M contract extension. He’s in the final year of that deal and the Colts will need to pony-up some cash if they want to keep him from hitting free agency. Seeing as how they may be looking to hit the reset button, that may be unlikely. How he can help Washington Some will say that 30 is old, but for offensive linemen, many of whom can play at an elite level well into their mid-thirties, Nelson is still in his prime. He’s been a pillar of that Indianapolis offense line, missing just four games over his career, so there are no current injury concerns. The Colts are rumored to be looking for a first-round pick in return for Nelson, but many have opined that a higher second-rounder could secure his services. Commanders GM Adam Peters hasn’t exactly knocked the cover off the ball with his second-round picks. He’s missed badly on Johnny Newton, Mike Sainristil and Ben Sinnott, and while Trey Amos showed promise as a rookie, he’s had a hard time staying healthy. Using a second-rounder to land Nelson does a few things for this struggling offense: It secures left guard (a position Washington has struggled to find consistency and solid play) for the foreseeable future. Nelson and Sam Cosmi give Washington arguably the league’s best guard tandem. With the return of Laremy Tunsil, the Commanders would have THREE Blues along the offensive line. Most importantly, he provides protection for Jayden Daniels and should make life easier in the rushing attack. Since he was drafted No. 2 overall in 2024, fans have literally BEGGED to surround Jayden with pieces, so he won’t have to play Superman every time he takes the field. Currently, through six weeks, Daniels is the most pressured quarterback in the NFL in time to throw. Trading for Nelson could help turn this around. Highest QB Pressure Rate: Jayden Daniels is running for his life in Washington 🚨 🌡️ Jayden Daniels 🌡️ Deshaun Watson 🌡️ Justin Herbert pic.twitter.com/JLYpNKOrrX — FTN (@FTNFantasy) October 23, 2026 Trading for Brian Thomas Jr. Brian Thomas Jr. is a 6’3” 210-pound athletic freak at wide receiver. Brian Thomas Jr. was drafted with pick 23 of round 1 in the 2024 draft class. He scored a 9.84 #RAS out of a possible 10.00. This ranked 57 out of 3402 WR from 1987 to 2024. https://t.co/UQzFM7GSyH pic.twitter.com/ggcBNi9iDp — RAS.football (@MathBomb) April 26, 2024 At just 24 years old, Thomas has the height/weight/speed combo that teams salivate over. As a rookie in Jacksonville, he went for 87-1,282-10. His stats fell off significantly in 2025 under head coach Liam Coen, and there were rumors he’d fallen out of favor with the coaching staff. Through six games this season, Thomas has just nine receptions for 105 yards and a touchdown. That offense now runs through Parker Washington, and it’s clear that Thomas needs a change of scenery. How he can help Washington After losing Terry McLaurin to a knee injury, Washington doesn’t have a true deep threat to help keep defenses honest. With 4.33 speed and the coveted size to boot, Thomas gives David Blough’s offense just that. He was taken 23rd overall in the 2024 NFL Draft so he still has two-and-a-half years of team control on his rookie deal. He played with Jayden Daniels at LSU, and the two are friends and have some prior chemistry. The rumor is the Jaguars are looking for a higher day-three pick in exchange for Thomas, but they are also in need of help along the interior defense line. There may be an opportunity to trade Daron Payne for Brian Thomas Jr. in a straight-up player-for-player deal. The Jaguars are looking to make a deep playoff push and they are not keen on trading Thomas Jr. to an AFC contender. Even before the injury, it was looking very unlikely that McLaurin would return to Washington in 2027. Diggs will be a free agent and is not part of the team’s long-term plans. That leaves just Antonio Williams, Jaylin Lane and Luke McCaffrey as the team’s top targets in 2027. Thomas has the talent which we all saw as a rookie. That doesn’t just disappear at 24 years of age. Reuniting him with his former LSU Tigers teammate could give him the chance to reenergize his career and take advantage of his many gifts. These are just two potential moves that Adam Peters could look to make at the trade deadline. However, based on Washington’s team needs and potential compensation having to be moved, these may make the most sense. Let’s discuss further in the comments section.

Mike Sainristil played seven defensive snaps against San Francisco; with Trey Amos back, earning more work will take more than a change in position [After playing] 54 of 55 defensive snaps against Philadelphia [in Week 1], six games into the season, finding a place for him has become a much different conversation. Sainristil played seven defensive snaps against San Francisco . Robertson played all 62, while Rasul Douglas and Trey Amos played 36 apiece. That leaves Washington entering its bye with three corners getting considerably more work than [the] player it drafted in the second round just two years ago. The coverage has been a problem. Entering Washington’s bye, Pro Football Focus gave Sainristil a 29.4 overall defensive grade and a 28.5 coverage grade, both ranking 102nd among 102 qualifying cornerbacks. When asked about Amos’ return and whether he had considered Sainristil at safety, [defensive coordinator Daronte] Jones pointed to the deep-zone assignments Sainristil had handled against New York . “The depth chart that we had in that game and who was available definitely had something to do with that,” Jones said. He was explaining how the team could use him in different assignments, without announcing a permanent position change. That’s where I would keep Sainristil for now: situational nickel work and reserve duties that allow Washington to use that flexibility when needed. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Riggo’s Rag Rasul Douglas is turning a late Commanders signing into an offseason steal The Commanders needed more from Douglas than they originally anticipated. Trey Amos spent the first four games on injured reserve and missed five contests before returning on Monday Night Football against the San Francisco 49ers. Mike Sainristil’s freefall has seen him become an afterthought, which was the only sensible call left. That meant Douglas had to step up and he’s coped with the challenge superbly. Douglas has been a tremendous addition. His coverage is an outstanding feature of his production, giving Washington the assurance it desperately needed. The 2017 third-round pick out of West Virginia is giving up just 54.5 percent of targets thrown in his direction. Douglas has five pass breakups and one interception. He is also allowing a measly 63.8 passer rating when targeted, which fairly reflects his outstanding consistency. That’s not all. Douglas is also making a considerable impression against the run. His physicality closer to the line of scrimmage goes overlooked, but it’s nonetheless impressive. Douglas has been credited with eight run stops through six games. And even with the Commanders’ defense struggling to maintain high performance for four quarters , almost nobody is gaining big yards on the ground. Other factors are in play. However, Douglas is one reason for this turnaround. Douglas only signed a one-year deal. He’s still performing at a high level, but he also recently turned 31. That’s not ancient, but it is the stage where corners tend to regress. That’s a problem on both sides of the ball for a team that has already seen close games slip away. The Commanders have scored nine touchdowns on 17 red-zone trips, or 52.9%, tied for 21st-best with the Bengals. Opposing teams have had five more trips (22 total) but scored nine more touchdowns (81.8%), which ranks Washington 31st in red-zone touchdown rate allowed through Week 6. Commanders Roundtable Three trade targets for the Washington Commanders [Tthe Commanders…sit two games back in an NFC East race that resembles 2020. With embattled head coach Dan Quinn and general manager Adam Peters potentially facing scrutiny for the roster construction, the pressure is on to make the right roster upgrades to give the team a chance to make a run in a suddenly compromised division. But who are trade targets? Amani Hooker, safety, Tennessee Titans Hooker, 28, has been the most underrated safety in the NFL because he is stuck on a struggling Titans team that’s winless this season and went 3-19 in the last two seasons. Hooker is a piece teams would like, as a productive player with one 92-yard interception and 28 tackles so far in 2026. His run defense grade per PFF is 86.5, the seventh among safeties, and his coverage grade is 62.1, the 37th among safeties, for a combined grade of 73.0, good for 21st out of 96 qualified safeties. Quan Martin and Jeremy Reeves haven’t shown they’re starting-quality safeties, and Hooker and Nick Cross would be a beneficial safety tandem for the next few seasons. Hooker is under contract through 2028 after signing a three-year extension before the 2025 season. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated Commanders’ Drew Stevens Owns Two Franchise Rookie Records After Just Six Games Washington Commanders rookie Drew Stevens already held the franchise’s rookie record for the longest field goal before Monday night against San Francisco. His 51-yarder in the first quarter brought him to three makes from 50-plus yards , extending the franchise rookie record he already held. The 57-yarder against Seattle set the distance record in Week 3, after Stevens had connected from 55 yards against Philadelphia in the opener. Both rookie marks are now his with 11 games still left to play. Stevens was 3-for-5 on field goals after the first two games, and he hasn’t missed one since. He made two apiece against Seattle, Indianapolis, and New York, then his lone attempt against San Francisco. That puts him at seven straight makes and 10-for-12 overall, or 83.3%, entering the bye. Both misses came from 50-plus yards during those opening two games. He’s also 7-for-7 inside 50 yards and 3-for-5 from 50 or longer. The long kicks are getting the records, but Stevens has taken care of the shorter field goals, too. His 57-yarder against Seattle came as the first half expired in a 33–31 win, so that range has already helped Washington pick up points in a game it barely won. title: Commanders survey results: Fans refuse to punt on 2026 season
summary: In this week’s Reacts survey, we asked Hogs Haven readers two questions regarding the state of the Washington Commanders as the team enters its Week 7 bye. A question of confidence The first question was our standard pulse check: Are you confident in the team’s direction? Interestingly, that 26% positive mark represents an 8-point jump […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MD - DECEMBER 30: Washington Redskins punter Tress Way (5) throws a completed pass on a fake punt in the third quarter against the Philadelphia Eagles at FedEx Field. (Photo by Jonathan Newton / The Washington Post via Getty Images) In this week’s Reacts survey, we asked Hogs Haven readers two questions regarding the state of the Washington Commanders as the team enters its Week 7 bye. A question of confidence The first question was our standard pulse check: Are you confident in the team’s direction? No: 74% Yes: 26% Interestingly, that 26% positive mark represents an 8-point jump from the 18% registered after Week 6 despite the Commanders suffering a second consecutive loss. While nearly three-quarters of the fanbase remains skeptical—understandably so after a grueling 1-4-1 start—the modest uptick suggests that a few days of distance from game action have allowed a little bit of perspective to seep back in. What Hogs Haven readers want to see from the team after the bye Our second question tackled the immediate road ahead: What do you want to see from the Commanders after the bye week? Rally around Dan Quinn, fight to win games, and reach the postseason: 64% An interim head coach to replace Dan Quinn and a shift in focus to the 2027 season: 36% Taken together, the results of the two survey questions tell a revealing story about where this fanbase stands at the mid-autumn break. While 3 out of 4 fans remain uneasy with the broader direction after six weeks of frustration, nearly two-thirds flatly reject the idea of waving a white flag on the 2026 campaign. There is a tangible difference between acknowledging a disappointing start and surrendering to it, and Hogs Haven readers clearly believe that letting Dan Quinn and this squad fight through the storm offers a far better path forward than triggering an organizational fire drill in late October. The case for measured optimism in the “second season” that starts after the bye To anyone staring strictly at the standings, talking about a postseason push might sound borderline delusional. The bad news from the first 6 weeks is well known, painful to recount, and needs little rehash here: missed opportunities, fourth-quarter breakdowns, and an offense that was severely hindered when quarterback injuries disrupted Weeks 2, 3, and 4. Yet, nearly two-thirds of our readers voted against pulling the rip cord. As Alex Rowsey aptly put it in the comments, it is hard to stomach punting on an NFL season when the NFC East remains completely up for grabs. Look around the neighborhood. The Philadelphia Eagles have lost Jalen Hurts for the rest of the season , have dropped 4 straight games, and look vulnerable heading into the Week 8 road game against Washington. The Dallas Cowboys , despite avoiding the quarterback injuries that partly-derailed Washington’s early slate, have also dropped 4 of their first 6 games and look just as out of sorts . Meanwhile, the New York Giants sit just 2 games ahead of Washington and enter this weekend as double-digit underdogs against the Houston Texans. Nobody is running away with this division. In fact, Washington’s remaining strength of schedule over the final 11 games is among the easiest in the NFL, which seems to open up a world of opportunity – if the team can make some meaningful improvements during this week’s lull in the action. FWIW via @tankathon only three teams have an easier remaining strength of schedule than the Commanders … unfortunately the Cowboys are one of em pic.twitter.com/9tfl8uZJhk — Mitchell Tischler (@Mitch_Tischler) October 20, 2026 The secret ingredient to success Most importantly, Jayden Daniels has played high-caliber football behind center and continues to display significant upside. As offensive coordinator David Blough and defensive coordinator Daronte Jones gain comfort and rhythm in their play-calling duties, the units around Daniels should improve steadily. If the coaching staff utilizes the bye week to incorporate more quick reads, rhythmic RPOs, and enhanced and aggressive defensive looks—points raised repeatedly by commenters and media—this team has plenty of room for meaningful growth. Dan Quinn, Josh Harris, and the executive reality In addition to the Reacts surveys we carry out on Hogs Haven, SB Nation conducts regular weekly national (even international) polling of fans across the fanbases of all 32 teams via email. This week, one of the national survey questions asked which coach would be the first to be fired this season. Visit our partners at FanDuel I think the national press and most NFL fans are reading the situation in Washington all wrong. It seems to me that a hell of a lot more would have to go wrong for the Washington ownership group to consider parting ways with DQ in the midst of his 3rd season. It’s true that a sizable 36% contingent voted for an interim coach to replace Quinn in our Reacts survey this week, and several commenters made thoughtful arguments about clock management and late-game execution. But owner Josh Harris is an experienced professional sports owner who understands the value of organizational stability. Harris knows all too well the damage caused by knee-jerk, emotional reactions to early-season adversity. There is an old, reliable axiom in professional management that applies to both business and sports: a good executive supports his guy 100% right up until the exact moment he doesn’t. That is not an empty cliché; it is how professional organizations operate — and Josh Harris knows how to run a professional organization. As long as Dan Quinn is the head coach of the Washington Commanders, he holds the complete, undivided support of ownership. Harris has shown throughout his ownership career that he prefers to evaluate a full body of work across an entire 17-game campaign rather than pulling the plug mid-stream. Quinn will be given every opportunity to navigate through these waters, and I would hope that fans will be pulling for him to succeed — our survey results indicate that most Hogs Haven readers will absolutely continue to root for the team to win games and earn a playoff spot. Personally, I expect Quinn to succeed in turning the 2026 season around, and I expect him to remain the head coach into 2027 after doing so. Consistent leadership and direction over a period of years has been proven to be more effective in the NFL than constantly lurching from one vision of leadership to another based on short term results. With 11 games left to play in the 2026 season, there’s a lot of time left to right the ship, but that opportunity would be lost if the mob mentality of “fire everyone” were to be adopted by Harris because of a tough few weeks to open the season. Charting the path back to relevance If you are looking for a reasonable roadmap to a season turnaround, consider how the next month sets up. Coming out of the bye, the Commanders face a wounded Philadelphia team, followed by the 2-4 Rams , and then a rematch with the Giants (who’ve just made the QB switch to JJ McCarthy). Winning those 3 games is entirely within reach, and doing so would vault Washington to 4-4-1, putting them right back at the .500 mark with 8 games to play. From there, the schedule remains exceptionally favorable. Winning 4 of the 6 winnable games between Weeks 11 and 16 (Bengals, Cardinals, Titans, Texans, Falcons, Vikings) would have Washington sitting two games above .500 heading into a pivotal Week 17 clash in Jacksonville. With one of the easiest remaining schedules in football ahead of them, the Commanders could put together a string of victories reminiscent of the 2012 Redskins ( from 3-6, 7 straight wins to close out the season ) or the 2015 team ( from 2-4, 6 wins in the final 8 games; 7 wins in the final 10 ). Heck, even the 2020 Football Team won a division title in a weak NFC East by going 5-2 in the final 7 games after a 2-7 start. We’ve seen the burgundy & gold turn mid-season losing teams into division…

full_text:
The throwbacks were well-represented in Week 6 of the NFL slate. While that's still the case this week, it's the alternates that lead the way -- including two monochromatic looks from the Houston Texans and Detroit Lions .

 

 Houston will be wearing its "battle red" combination, which the team first unveiled in 2024. It's all red from head to toe complete with a similarly colored matte lid that includes a new bullhorn logo. The numbers are deep steel blue with a liberty white trim, while the red pants boast blue and white stripes. The  New York Giants will counter with all-white. 

 Also unveiled in 2024, the Lions are rocking their all-black threads against the Green Bay Packers . The black jersey and pants include a Honolulu Blue matte helmet with leaping Lions logo in silver. There's also a black stripe across the middle. Detroit first wore black uniforms in 1948 before bringing it back in 2005 as an alternate. The team stopped wearing them after the 2007 season before returning it in 2024. 

 The Dallas Cowboys will don their color rush look against the Philadelphia Eagles on "Monday Night Football." Dallas unveiled these threads in 2015 with a silver helmet before an arctic white one debuted in 2022. The all-white combination has navy blue numbers and on the shoulder for a neat look.

 Though alternates are the headliners, fans of the classics aren't leaving empty handed either in Week 7.

 The Seattle Seahawks are wearing their throwbacks from the 1990s, complete with royal blue jerseys and silver pants and helmet. Seattle wore them last week on "Thursday Night Football." For the first time this season, the Atlanta Falcons and New York Jets are rocking classic uniforms. New York's is appropriately named "The Classic," and the all-white look pays homage to the 1968 championship season. It also includes uniform details from 1998 to 2018. Atlanta's threads include its iconic red helmet, which dates back to the 1960s, with black jerseys and white pants. 

 The first NFL game in Paris brings a first in the uniform department for the Pittsburgh Steelers .
